If music be the food of love, play on, / Give me excess of it; that, surfeiting, / The appetite may sicken and so die.— / That strain again;—it had a dying fall; / O, it came o'er my ear like the sweet south, / That breathes upon a bank of violets, / Stealing and giving odour.—Enough; no more; / 'Tis not so sweet now as it was before. / O spirit of love, how quick and fresh art thou! / That, notwithstanding thy capacity / Receiveth as the sea, nought enters there, / Of what validity and pitch soever, / But falls into abatement and low price / Even in a minute! so full of shapes is fancy, / That it alone is high-fantastical.

If music is what feeds love, keep playing. Give me too much of it, so that my appetite, overfed, grows sick and dies. Play that tune again; it had a falling, dying close. Oh, it reached my ear like a soft south wind breathing over a bank of violets, taking their scent and carrying it on. Enough, no more; it isn't as sweet now as it was before. Oh spirit of love, how restless and hungry you are! Although you can swallow as much as the sea, nothing enters you, however fine and high its value, that doesn't lose its worth within a minute! Desire is so full of changing shapes that nothing is more fantastical.
Will you go hunt, my lord?
Will you go hunting, my lord?

Why, so I do, the noblest that I have: / O, when mine eyes did see Olivia first, / Methought she purg'd the air of pestilence; / That instant was I turn'd into a hart; / And my desires, like fell and cruel hounds, / E'er since pursue me.—How now! what news from her?

Why, I am doing that already, with the noblest heart I have. Oh, when I first saw Olivia, I thought she cleansed the air of disease. At that moment I was turned into a hunted deer, and my desires, like fierce and cruel hounds, have chased me ever since. Now then, what news from her?

So please my lord, I might not be admitted, / But from her handmaid do return this answer: / The element itself, till seven years' heat, / Shall not behold her face at ample view; / But like a cloistress she will veiled walk, / And water once a-day her chamber round / With eye-offending brine: all this to season / A brother's dead love, which she would keep fresh / And lasting in her sad remembrance.

If it please you, my lord, I wasn't allowed in, but her maid gave me this answer. The sky itself won't see her face openly until seven summers have passed; she will walk veiled like a nun and wet her room once a day with stinging tears. All this is to preserve her love for her dead brother, which she wants to keep fresh and lasting in her sad memory.

O, she that hath a heart of that fine frame / To pay this debt of love but to a brother, / How will she love when the rich golden shaft / Hath kill'd the flock of all affections else / That live in her; when liver, brain, and heart, / These sovereign thrones, are all supplied and fill'd,— / Her sweet perfections,—with one self king!— / Away before me to sweet beds of flowers: / Love-thoughts lie rich when canopied with bowers.

Oh, if she has a heart so finely made that she pays this debt of love just to a brother, how will she love when Cupid's golden arrow has killed every other feeling that lives in her, when her liver, brain and heart, those royal thrones of passion, thought and feeling, are all filled and ruled by one single king! Go ahead of me to sweet beds of flowers; thoughts of love grow rich under a canopy of leaves.
And what should I do in Illyria? / My brother he is in Elysium. / Perchance he is not drown'd—What think you, sailors?
And what am I to do in Illyria? My brother is in heaven. Perhaps he isn't drowned. What do you think, sailors?
It is perchance that you yourself were sav'd.
It was only by chance that you yourself were saved.
O my poor brother! and so perchance may he be.
Oh my poor brother! Then perhaps by chance he was too.

True, madam; and, to comfort you with chance, / Assure yourself, after our ship did split, / When you, and those poor number sav'd with you, / Hung on our driving boat, I saw your brother, / Most provident in peril, bind himself,— / Courage and hope both teaching him the practice,— / To a strong mast that liv'd upon the sea; / Where, like Arion on the dolphin's back, / I saw him hold acquaintance with the waves / So long as I could see.

True, madam, and to comfort you with that chance, be sure of this: after our ship split, when you and the few saved with you were clinging to our drifting boat, I saw your brother, very sensible in danger, tie himself (courage and hope taught him how) to a strong mast that floated on the sea. There, like Arion riding the dolphin, I saw him keep company with the waves for as long as I could see him.
For saying so, there's gold! / Mine own escape unfoldeth to my hope, / Whereto thy speech serves for authority, / The like of him. Know'st thou this country?
For telling me that, here's gold! My own escape gives me hope, and your words support it, that he escaped too. Do you know this country?
Ay, madam, well; for I was bred and born / Not three hours' travel from this very place.
Yes, madam, well; I was born and raised less than three hours' journey from this very spot.
A noble duke, in nature / As in name.
A noble duke, noble by nature as well as by name.
Orsino! I have heard my father name him. / He was a bachelor then.
Orsino! I have heard my father mention him. He was a bachelor then.

And so is now, / Or was so very late; for but a month / Ago I went from hence; and then 'twas fresh / In murmur,—as, you know, what great ones do, / The less will prattle of,—that he did seek / The love of fair Olivia.

And he still is, or was very recently. When I left here only a month ago, there was fresh gossip (you know how ordinary people chatter about what great people do) that he was courting the beautiful Olivia.

A virtuous maid, the daughter of a count / That died some twelvemonth since; then leaving her / In the protection of his son, her brother, / Who shortly also died; for whose dear love, / They say, she hath abjured the company / And sight of men.

A virtuous young woman, the daughter of a count who died about a year ago. He left her in the care of his son, her brother, who soon died too. For love of him, they say, she has sworn off the company and even the sight of men.
O that I served that lady! / And might not be delivered to the world, / Till I had made mine own occasion mellow, / What my estate is.
Oh, if only I could serve that lady, and not have the world know who I am until I've made my own moment ripe for it!
That were hard to compass: / Because she will admit no kind of suit, / No, not the duke's.
That would be hard to arrange, because she won't receive any kind of request, not even the Duke's.

There is a fair behaviour in thee, captain; / And though that nature with a beauteous wall / Doth oft close in pollution, yet of thee / I will believe thou hast a mind that suits / With this thy fair and outward character. / I pray thee, and I'll pay thee bounteously, / Conceal me what I am; and be my aid / For such disguise as, haply, shall become / The form of my intent. I'll serve this duke; / Thou shalt present me as an eunuch to him; / It may be worth thy pains, for I can sing, / And speak to him in many sorts of music, / That will allow me very worth his service. / What else may hap to time I will commit; / Only shape thou silence to my wit.

There is a good honesty in your manner, captain. Although nature often hides corruption behind a beautiful outside, I will believe that your mind matches your fair appearance. I beg you, and I'll pay you generously, hide who I am and help me with a disguise that suits my plan. I'll serve this duke. You will present me to him as a eunuch; it will be worth your trouble, because I can sing and play him many kinds of music, which will make me worth employing. Whatever else happens I'll leave to time. Just keep quiet and fit in with my scheme.
Be you his eunuch and your mute I'll be; / When my tongue blabs, then let mine eyes not see.
You be his eunuch and I'll be your mute. If my tongue ever blabs, may my eyes go blind.
I thank thee. Lead me on.
What a plague means my niece, to take the death of her / brother thus? I am sure care's an enemy to life.
What the plague does my niece mean by taking her brother's death like this? I'm sure that grief is bad for your health.
By my troth, Sir Toby, you must come in earlier o' nights; / your cousin, my lady, takes great exceptions to your ill hours.
Honestly, Sir Toby, you must come in earlier at night. Your relative, my lady, strongly objects to your late hours.
Why, let her except, before excepted.
Well, let her object all she likes, as the lawyers say.
Ay, but you must confine yourself within the modest limits / of order.
Yes, but you must keep yourself within the decent limits of good order.
Confine? I'll confine myself no finer than I am: these / clothes are good enough to drink in, and so be these boots too; / an they be not, let them hang themselves in their own straps.
Keep myself in? I'll not make myself any neater than I am. These clothes are good enough to drink in, and so are these boots. If they aren't, let them hang themselves by their own straps.
That quaffing and drinking will undo you: I heard my lady / talk of it yesterday; and of a foolish knight that you brought in / one night here to be her wooer.
All this guzzling and drinking will ruin you. I heard my lady talking about it yesterday, and about a foolish knight you brought here one night to court her.
He's as tall a man as any's in Illyria.
He's as fine a man as anyone in Illyria.
What's that got to do with it?
Why, he has three thousand ducats a year.
Why, he has an income of three thousand ducats a year.
Ay, but he'll have but a year in all these ducats; he's a / very fool, and a prodigal.
Yes, but those ducats will only last him a year. He's a complete fool and a spendthrift.
Fye that you'll say so! he plays o' the viol-de-gambo, / and speaks three or four languages word for word without book, / and hath all the good gifts of nature.
Shame on you for saying so! He plays the viola da gamba, speaks three or four languages word for word without a book, and has every natural gift.

He hath indeed,—almost natural: for, besides that he's a / fool, he's a great quarreller; and, but that he hath the gift of / a coward to allay the gust he hath in quarrelling, 'tis thought / among the prudent he would quickly have the gift of a grave.

He has indeed: he's almost a natural idiot. Besides being a fool, he's a great one for picking quarrels, and if he didn't have a coward's gift for cooling his appetite for fighting, sensible people think he'd soon have the gift of a grave.
By this hand, they are scoundrels and subtractors that / say so of him. Who are they?
By this hand, the people who say that about him are scoundrels and detractors. Who are they?
They that add, moreover, he's drunk nightly in your company.
The same people who add that he's drunk every night in your company.

With drinking healths to my niece; I'll drink to her as / long as there is a passage in my throat and drink in Illyria. / He's a coward and a coystril that will not drink to my niece / till his brains turn o' the toe like a parish-top. What, wench! / Castiliano-vulgo! for here comes Sir Andrew Ague-face.

From drinking toasts to my niece. I'll drink to her as long as there's a passage in my throat and drink in Illyria. Any man who won't drink to my niece till his head spins like a top is a coward and a low knave. Look out, girl! Best behaviour! Here comes Sir Andrew Agueface.
Sir Toby Belch! how now, Sir Toby Belch!
Sir Toby Belch! How are you, Sir Toby Belch!
Good Mistress Accost, I desire better acquaintance.
Good Mistress Accost, I'd like to know you better.
You mistake, knight: accost is, front her, board her, / woo her, assail her.
You've got it wrong, knight. To accost means to face her, board her, woo her, attack her.
By my troth, I would not undertake her in this company. / Is that the meaning of accost?
Honestly, I wouldn't take her on in front of all these people. Is that what accost means?
An thou let part so, Sir Andrew, would thou mightst never / draw sword again.
If you let her leave like that, Sir Andrew, I hope you never draw your sword again.
An you part so, mistress, I would I might never draw / sword again. Fair lady, do you think you have fools in hand?
If you leave like that, mistress, I hope I never draw my sword again. Fair lady, do you think you are dealing with fools?
Sir, I have not you by the hand.
Sir, I don't have you by the hand.
Marry, but you shall have; and here's my hand.
Well, you shall have, and here's my hand.
Now, sir, thought is free. I pray you, bring your hand to / the buttery-bar and let it drink.
Now, sir, I can think what I like. Please, bring your hand to the bar of the pantry and let it have a drink.
Why, sweetheart? What does your figure of speech mean?
Why, I think so; I am not such an ass but I can keep my / hand dry. But what's your jest?
Why, I think so. I'm not such an ass that I can't keep my hand dry. But what's your joke?
Ay, sir, I have them at my fingers' ends: marry, now I let / go your hand I am barren.
Yes, sir, I have them at my fingertips. But now that I let go of your hand, I'm empty.
O knight, thou lack'st a cup of canary: When did I see / thee so put down?
Oh knight, you need a cup of sweet wine. When have I ever seen you so knocked down?

Never in your life, I think; unless you see canary put / me down. Methinks sometimes I have no more wit than a Christian / or an ordinary man has; but I am great eater of beef, and, I / believe, that does harm to my wit.

Never in your life, I think, unless you've seen wine knock me down. Sometimes I think I have no more wit than an ordinary Christian or any common man. But I'm a great eater of beef, and I believe that harms my wits.
An I thought that, I'd forswear it. I'll ride home / to-morrow, Sir Toby.
If I thought that, I'd give it up. I'll ride home tomorrow, Sir Toby.
What is pourquoy? do or not do? I would I had bestowed / that time in the tongues that I have in fencing, dancing, and / bear-baiting. Oh, had I but followed the arts!
What does 'pourquoi' mean? Go or don't go? I wish I had spent the time on languages that I've spent on fencing, dancing and bear-baiting. Oh, if only I'd studied the arts!
Then hadst thou had an excellent head of hair.
Then you would have had an excellent head of hair.
Why, would that have mended my hair?
Why, would that have improved my hair?
Past question; for thou seest it will not curl by nature.
No question, because you can see it won't curl naturally.
But it becomes me well enough, does't not?
But it suits me well enough, doesn't it?
Excellent; it hangs like flax on a distaff; and I hope to / see a houswife take thee between her legs and spin it off.
Excellent. It hangs like flax on a spinning stick, and I hope to see a housewife take you between her legs and spin it off.
Faith, I'll home to-morrow, Sir Toby; your niece will / not be seen; or, if she be, it's four to one she'll none of me; / the count himself here hard by woos her.
Honestly, I'll go home tomorrow, Sir Toby. Your niece won't see anyone, or if she does, it's four to one she won't have me. The Count himself, close by here, is wooing her.
She'll none o' the Count; she'll not match above her / degree, neither in estate, years, nor wit; I have heard her / swear't. Tut, there's life in't, man.
She won't have the Count. She won't marry above her own rank, in wealth, age or intelligence; I've heard her swear it. Come on, there's still hope, man.
I'll stay a month longer. I am a fellow o' the strangest / mind i' the world; I delight in masques and revels sometimes / altogether.
I'll stay a month longer. I'm a man with the strangest mind in the world; I sometimes love masked balls and parties more than anything.
Art thou good at these kick-shaws, knight?
Are you good at these trifles, knight?
As any man in Illyria, whatsoever he be, under the / degree of my betters; and yet I will not compare with an old man.
As good as any man in Illyria, whoever he is, as long as he isn't my superior; and yet I won't compare myself with an expert.
What is thy excellence in a galliard, knight?
How good are you at the galliard, knight?
Faith, I can cut a caper.
Honestly, I can cut a caper.
And I can cut the mutton to't.
And I can cut the mutton to go with it.
And, I think, I have the back-trick simply as strong as / any man in Illyria.
And I think I can do the backward step as well as any man in Illyria.

Wherefore are these things hid? wherefore have these / gifts a curtain before them? are they like to take dust, like / Mistress Mall's picture? why dost thou not go to church in a / galliard and come home in a coranto? My very walk should be a / jig; I would not so much as make water but in a sink-a-pace. What / dost thou mean? is it a world to hide virtues in? I did think, by / the excellent constitution of thy leg, it was formed under the / star of a galliard.

Why are these talents hidden? Why do these gifts have a curtain in front of them? Are they likely to gather dust, like some lady's portrait? Why don't you go to church dancing a galliard and come home in a running dance? My very walk would be a jig; I wouldn't even piss except in a five-step dance. What do you mean by it? Is this a world to hide your virtues in? Judging by the excellent shape of your leg, I thought it was formed under a dancing star.
Ay, 'tis strong, and it does indifferent well in / flame-colour'd stock. Shall we set about some revels?
Yes, it's strong, and it looks pretty good in a flame-coloured stocking. Shall we start some partying?
What shall we do else? were we not born under Taurus?
What else would we do? Weren't we born under Taurus?
Taurus? That rules the sides and the heart.
No, sir; it is legs and thighs. Let me see thee caper: ha, / higher: ha, ha!—excellent!
No, sir, it rules the legs and thighs. Let me see you jump. Ha, higher! Ha, ha! Excellent!
If the duke continue these favours towards you, Cesario, / you are like to be much advanced; he hath known you but three / days, and already you are no stranger.
If the Duke keeps showing you these favours, Cesario, you're likely to go far. He has only known you three days, and already you're no stranger.
You either fear his humour or my negligence, that you call / in question the continuance of his love. Is he inconstant, sir, / in his favours?
You must fear either his moods or my carelessness, if you question whether his affection will last. Is he changeable in his favours, sir?
I thank you. Here comes the count.
Thank you. Here comes the Count.
On your attendance, my lord; here.
Here, my lord, at your service.

Stand you awhile aloof.—Cesario, / Thou know'st no less but all; I have unclasp'd / To thee the book even of my secret soul: / Therefore, good youth, address thy gait unto her; / Be not denied access, stand at her doors, / And tell them there thy fixed foot shall grow / Till thou have audience.

Stand aside for a while. Cesario, you know everything; I have opened to you the book of my most secret soul. So, good youth, take yourself to her. Don't be refused entry; stand at her doors and tell them your foot will take root there until you are heard.
Sure, my noble lord, / If she be so abandon'd to her sorrow / As it is spoke, she never will admit me.
Surely, my noble lord, if she is as lost in grief as people say, she will never let me in.
Be clamorous and leap all civil bounds, / Rather than make unprofited return.
Make a noise and break every rule of politeness rather than come back with nothing.
Say I do speak with her, my lord. What then?
Suppose I do speak with her, my lord. What then?

O, then unfold the passion of my love, / Surprise her with discourse of my dear faith: / It shall become thee well to act my woes; / She will attend it better in thy youth / Than in a nuncio of more grave aspect.

Oh, then reveal my passionate love and overwhelm her with talk of my devotion. It will suit you well to act out my suffering; she will listen to it better from a youth like you than from a messenger with a more serious face.
I think not so, my lord.
I don't think so, my lord.

Dear lad, believe it, / For they shall yet belie thy happy years / That say thou art a man: Diana's lip / Is not more smooth and rubious; thy small pipe / Is as the maiden's organ, shrill and sound, / And all is semblative a woman's part. / I know thy constellation is right apt / For this affair:—some four or five attend him: / All, if you will; for I myself am best / When least in company:—prosper well in this, / And thou shalt live as freely as thy lord, / To call his fortunes thine.

Dear boy, believe it. Anyone who says you are a man doesn't know your youth: the goddess Diana's lips are not smoother or redder than yours, and your little voice is like a girl's, high and clear, and everything about you looks like a woman's part. I know your stars make you just right for this business. Four or five of you go with him, or all of you if you like, since I'm happiest when I have least company. Succeed in this, and you will live as freely as your lord and share his fortune as your own.
I'll do my best / To woo your lady. [Aside] Yet, a barful strife! / Whoe'er I woo, myself would be his wife.
I'll do my best to woo your lady. [Aside] Yet what a struggle! Whoever I woo for him, I'd like to be his wife myself.
Nay; either tell me where thou hast been, or I will not open / my lips so wide as a bristle may enter in way of thy excuse: my / lady will hang thee for thy absence.
No, either tell me where you've been or I won't open my lips wide enough to let a hair through in your defence. My lady will hang you for being away.
Let her hang me: he that is well hanged in this world needs / to fear no colours.
Let her hang me. A man who is well hanged in this world doesn't need to fear any enemy's flags.
He shall see none to fear.
He won't see any to be afraid of.
A good lenten answer: I can tell thee where that saying was / born, of, I fear no colours.
A thin, meagre answer. I can tell you where that saying 'I fear no colours' came from.
In the wars; and that may you be bold to say in your foolery.
From the wars, and you can be bold enough to say so in your fooling.
Well, God give them wisdom that have it; and those that are / fools, let them use their talents.
Well, God give wisdom to those who have it; and as for fools, let them use the talents they have.
Yet you will be hanged for being so long absent: or to be / turned away; is not that as good as a hanging to you?
Still, you'll be hanged for being away so long, or else thrown out. Isn't that as good as a hanging to you?
Many a good hanging prevents a bad marriage; and for turning / away, let summer bear it out.
Many a good hanging prevents a bad marriage; and as for being thrown out, the summer will make that bearable.
Not so, neither: but I am resolved on two points.
Not exactly, but I am fixed on two points.
That if one break, the other will hold; or if both break, / your gaskins fall.
So that if one breaks, the other will hold; or if both break, your trousers fall down.
Apt, in good faith, very apt! Well, go thy way; if Sir Toby / would leave drinking, thou wert as witty a piece of Eve's flesh / as any in Illyria.
Clever, honestly, very clever! Well, off you go. If Sir Toby would give up drinking, you'd be as witty a daughter of Eve as any in Illyria.
Peace, you rogue; no more o' that; here comes my lady: make / your excuse wisely; you were best.
Quiet, you rogue, no more of that. Here comes my lady. You'd better make your excuse wisely.

Wit, and't be thy will, put me into good fooling! Those wits / that think they have thee do very oft prove fools; and I, that am / sure I lack thee, may pass for a wise man. For what says / Quinapalus? Better a witty fool than a foolish wit.—God bless / thee, lady!

Wit, if it's your will, help me fool well! Clever people who think they have you often turn out to be fools; and I, who am sure I lack you, may pass for a wise man. For what does the philosopher Quinapalus say? 'Better a witty fool than a foolish wit.' God bless you, lady!
Do you not hear, fellows? Take away the lady.
Don't you hear, fellows? Take away the lady.
Go to, you're a dry fool; I'll no more of you: besides, you / grow dishonest.
Enough; you're a dull fool. I've had enough of you. Besides, you're becoming unreliable.

Two faults, madonna, that drink and good counsel will amend: / for give the dry fool drink, then is the fool not dry; bid the / dishonest man mend himself: if he mend, he is no longer / dishonest; if he cannot, let the botcher mend him. Anything / that's mended is but patched; virtue that transgresses is but / patched with sin, and sin that amends is but patched with virtue. / If that this simple syllogism will serve, so; if it will not, / what remedy? As there is no true cuckold but calamity, so / beauty's a flower:—the lady bade take away the fool; therefore, / I say again, take her away.

Two faults, madonna, that drink and good advice will cure. Give the dry fool a drink, and then the fool is not dry. Tell the dishonest man to mend his ways: if he mends, he is no longer dishonest; if he can't, let the tailor mend him. Anything that's mended is only patched: virtue that goes wrong is only patched with sin, and sin that reforms is only patched with virtue. If this simple logic works, good; if it doesn't, what can be done? Just as the only true cuckold is misfortune, so beauty is a flower that fades. The lady said take away the fool; so, I say again, take her away.
Sir, I bade them take away you.
Sir, I told them to take away you.
Misprision in the highest degree!—Lady, Cucullus non facit / monachum; that's as much to say, I wear not motley in my / brain. Good madonna, give me leave to prove you a fool.
A mistake of the highest order! Lady, 'the hood does not make the monk', which is as much as to say that I don't wear a fool's costume in my brain. Good madonna, let me prove that you are a fool.
I must catechize you for it, madonna. / Good my mouse of virtue, answer me.
I must question you like a catechism, madonna. My good little mouse of virtue, answer me.
Well, sir, for want of other idleness, I'll 'bide your proof.
Well, sir, since I have nothing better to do, I'll put up with your proof.
Good madonna, why are you in mourning?
Good fool, for my brother's death.
Good fool, because my brother has died.
I think his soul is in hell, madonna.
I think his soul is in hell, madonna.
I know his soul is in heaven, fool.
I know his soul is in heaven, fool.
The more fool you, madonna, to mourn for your brother's soul / being in heaven.—Take away the fool, gentlemen.
Then you're even more of a fool, madonna, to mourn for your brother's soul when it's in heaven. Take away the fool, gentlemen.
What think you of this fool, Malvolio? doth he not mend?
What do you think of this fool, Malvolio? Isn't he improving?
Yes; and shall do, till the pangs of death shake him. / Infirmity, that decays the wise, doth ever make the better fool.
Yes, and he will keep improving until the pains of death shake him. Old age, which makes the wise decay, always makes a fool better at being a fool.
God send you, sir, a speedy infirmity, for the better / increasing your folly! Sir Toby will be sworn that I am no fox; / but he will not pass his word for twopence that you are no fool.
God send you an early old age, sir, to increase your foolishness! Sir Toby will swear that I'm no fox, but he won't bet twopence that you're no fool.
How say you to that, Malvolio?
What do you say to that, Malvolio?

I marvel your ladyship takes delight in such a barren / rascal; I saw him put down the other day with an ordinary fool / that has no more brain than a stone. Look you now, he's out of / his guard already; unless you laugh and minister occasion to him, / he is gagged. I protest I take these wise men that crow so at / these set kind of fools, no better than the fools' zanies.

I'm amazed that your ladyship enjoys such an empty-headed rascal. I saw him beaten the other day in a battle of wits by an ordinary fool who has no more brain than a stone. Look at him now, he's already lost for words. Unless you laugh and give him openings, he's dumbstruck. I declare that I consider these wise men who crow with delight at these trained fools no better than the fools' stooges.

O, you are sick of self-love, Malvolio, and taste with a / distempered appetite. To be generous, guiltless, and of free / disposition, is to take those things for bird-bolts that you deem / cannon bullets. There is no slander in an allowed fool, though he / do nothing but rail; nor no railing in known discreet man, though / he do nothing but reprove.

Oh, you are sick with self-love, Malvolio, and you taste everything with a sickly appetite. Being generous, innocent and good-natured means taking things you think are cannonballs as if they were blunt toy arrows. There's no slander in a licensed fool, even if he does nothing but mock; just as there's no mockery in a man known to be sensible, even if he does nothing but criticise.
Now Mercury endue thee with leasing, for thou speakest well of / fools!
Now may Mercury, god of tricksters, teach you how to lie, because you speak well of fools!
Madam, there is at the gate a young gentleman much desires / to speak with you.
Madam, there's a young gentleman at the gate who very much wants to speak with you.
From the Count Orsino, is it?
I know not, madam; 'tis a fair young man, and well attended.
I don't know, madam. He's a handsome young man, with a good number of attendants.
Who of my people hold him in delay?
Which of my household is keeping him waiting?
Fetch him off, I pray you; he speaks nothing but madman. / Fie on him!
Get him away from there, please; he talks nothing but nonsense. Shame on him!
Go you, Malvolio: if it be a suit from the count, I am sick, or / not at home; what you will to dismiss it.
You go, Malvolio. If it's a message from the Count, I'm sick or not at home; say whatever you like to get rid of him.
Now you see, sir, how your fooling grows old, and people dislike / it.
Now you see, sir, how your fooling has grown stale, and people dislike it.
Thou hast spoke for us, madonna, as if thy eldest son should / be a fool: whose skull Jove cram with brains, for here he comes— / one of thy kin, has a most weak pia mater.
You have spoken up for us fools, madonna, as if your eldest son were going to be a fool. May Jove cram his skull with brains, because here comes one of your relatives who has a very weak brain.
By mine honour, half drunk!—What is he at the gate, cousin?
Upon my honour, half drunk! Who is at the gate, cousin?
'Tis a gentleman here.—A plague o' these pickle-herrings!—How / now, sot?
There's a gentleman here. A plague on these pickled herrings! Well now, you idiot?
Cousin, cousin, how have you come so early by this lethargy?
Cousin, cousin, how did you come to be so sluggish so early in the day?
Lechery! I defy lechery. There's one at the gate.
Lechery! I defy lechery. There's someone at the gate.
Yes indeed, but who is he?
Let him be the devil an he will, I care not: give me / faith, say I. Well, it's all one.
Let him be the devil if he wants, I don't care. Give me faith, I say. Well, it's all the same.
What's a drunken man like, fool?
What is a drunk man like, fool?
Like a drowned man, a fool, and a madman: one draught above / heat makes him a fool; the second mads him; and a third drowns / him.
Like a drowned man, a fool and a madman. One drink too many makes him a fool, the second makes him mad, and a third drowns him.
Go thou and seek the coroner, and let him sit o' my coz; / for he's in the third degree of drink; he's drowned: go, look / after him.
Go and find the coroner and let him hold an inquest on my cousin, because he's in the third stage of drink: he's drowned. Go and look after him.
He is but mad yet, madonna; and the fool shall look to the / madman.
He's only mad so far, madonna, and the fool will look after the madman.

Madam, yond young fellow swears he will speak with you. I / told him you were sick; he takes on him to understand so much, / and therefore comes to speak with you; I told him you were / asleep; he seems to have a foreknowledge of that too, and / therefore comes to speak with you. What is to be said to him, / lady? he's fortified against any denial.

Madam, that young fellow swears he will speak with you. I told him you were sick; he claims he knows that, and so he has come to speak with you. I told him you were asleep; he seems to have known that already too, and so he has come to speak with you. What shall we say to him, lady? He is armed against every refusal.
Tell him, he shall not speak with me.
Tell him he will not speak with me.
Has been told so; and he says he'll stand at your door / like a sheriff's post, and be the supporter of a bench, but he'll / speak with you.
He's been told so, and he says he'll stand at your door like a post outside a sheriff's house, or prop up a bench, but he will speak with you.
What kind of man is he?
What kind of man is he?
Of very ill manner; he'll speak with you, will you or no.
A very ill-mannered sort. He'll speak with you whether you want to or not.
Of what personage and years is he?
What does he look like, and how old is he?

Not yet old enough for a man, nor young enough for a boy; / as a squash is before 'tis a peascod, or a codling, when 'tis / almost an apple: 'tis with him e'en standing water, between boy / and man. He is very well-favoured, and he speaks very shrewishly; / one would think his mother's milk were scarce out of him.

Not old enough to be a man, nor young enough to be a boy; like a pea pod before the peas form, or an unripe apple that's nearly an apple. He's at the turn of the tide, between boy and man. He's very good-looking, and he speaks very sharply; you'd think his mother's milk was hardly out of him.
Let him approach. Call in my gentlewoman.
Let him come in. Call my lady-in-waiting.
Gentlewoman, my lady is calling you.
Give me my veil; come, throw it o'er my face; / We'll once more hear Orsino's embassy.
Give me my veil. Come, throw it over my face. We'll hear Orsino's message once more.
The honourable lady of the house, which is she?
Which of you is the honourable lady of the house?
Speak to me; I shall answer for her. Your will?
Speak to me; I'll answer for her. What do you want?

Most radiant, exquisite, and unmatchable beauty,—I pray you, / tell me if this be the lady of the house, for I never saw her: I / would be loath to cast away my speech; for, besides that it is / excellently well penned, I have taken great pains to con it. Good / beauties, let me sustain no scorn; I am very comptible, even to / the least sinister usage.

Most radiant, exquisite and unequalled beauty... Please tell me if this is the lady of the house, because I have never seen her. I'd hate to waste my speech, because besides being extremely well written, I have taken great trouble to learn it by heart. Good beauties, don't mock me; I am very sensitive, even to the slightest unkindness.
Where have you come from, sir?
I can say little more than I have studied, and that / question's out of my part. Good gentle one, give me modest / assurance, if you be the lady of the house, that I may proceed in / my speech.
I can say little more than I have learned, and that question isn't in my part. Gentle lady, give me reasonable assurance that you are the lady of the house, so that I may go on with my speech.
No, my profound heart: and yet, by the very fangs of malice / I swear, I am not that I play. Are you the lady of the house?
No, my wise lady; and yet, I swear by the very fangs of malice, I am not what I am playing. Are you the lady of the house?
If I do not usurp myself, I am.
If I am not stealing my own place, I am.

Most certain, if you are she, you do usurp yourself; for / what is yours to bestow is not yours to reserve. But this is from / my commission: I will on with my speech in your praise, and then / show you the heart of my message.

If you are she, then you are certainly stealing from yourself, because what is yours to give away is not yours to keep. But this isn't part of my instructions. I'll go on with my speech in your praise, and then show you the heart of my message.
Come to what is important in't: I forgive you the praise.
Get to the important part; I'll excuse you the praise.
Alas, I took great pains to study it, and 'tis poetical.
Oh dear, I took great trouble to learn it, and it's poetic.

It is the more like to be feigned; I pray you keep it in. I / heard you were saucy at my gates; and allowed your approach, / rather to wonder at you than to hear you. If you be not mad, be / gone; if you have reason, be brief: 'tis not that time of moon / with me to make one in so skipping a dialogue.

Then it's all the more likely to be false; please keep it to yourself. I heard you were rude at my gates, and I let you in more to marvel at you than to listen to you. If you aren't mad, go; if you are sane, be brief. I'm not in the mood to take part in such a light-headed conversation.
Will you hoist sail, sir? here lies your way.
Will you set sail, sir? Here's your way out.
No, good swabber; I am to hull here a little longer.— / Some mollification for your giant, sweet lady.
No, good deck-scrubber, I'll stay anchored here a little longer. Please calm down your giant, sweet lady.
Tell me what you have to say.
Sure, you have some hideous matter to deliver, when the / courtesy of it is so fearful. Speak your office.
You must have something terrible to deliver, when the manner of it is so alarming. State your business.
It alone concerns your ear. I bring no overture of war, no / taxation of homage; I hold the olive in my hand: my words are as / full of peace as matter.
It concerns your ears alone. I bring no declaration of war and no demand for tribute. I hold the olive branch in my hand; my words are full of peace as well as substance.
Yet you began rudely. What are you? what would you?
Yet you began rudely. Who are you? What do you want?
The rudeness that hath appeared in me have I learned from my / entertainment. What I am and what I would are as secret as / maidenhead: to your ears, divinity; to any other's, profanation.
Any rudeness in me I learned from how I was received. Who I am and what I want are as private as virginity: to your ears, holy; to anyone else's, profane.
Give us the place alone: we will hear this divinity.
Leave us alone; we will hear this holy message.
Now, sir, what is your text?
Now, sir, what is your text?
A comfortable doctrine, and much may be said of it. / Where lies your text?
A comforting doctrine, and there's much to say about it. Where is your text found?
In his bosom? In what chapter of his bosom?
In his heart? In which chapter of his heart?
To answer by the method, in the first of his heart.
To answer in the same style, in the first chapter of his heart.
O, I have read it; it is heresy. Have you no more to say?
Oh, I have read it; it's heresy. Have you nothing more to say?
Good madam, let me see your face.
Good madam, let me see your face.

Have you any commission from your lord to negotiate with my / face? you are now out of your text: but we will draw the curtain / and show you the picture. Look you, sir, such a one I was this / present. Is't not well done?

Has your lord told you to negotiate with my face? Now you've strayed from your text. But we'll draw back the curtain and show you the picture. Look, sir, this is what I looked like at this present moment. Isn't it well painted?
Excellently done, if God did all.
Excellently painted, if God did it all.
'Tis in grain, sir; 'twill endure wind and weather.
The colour is fast, sir; it will last through wind and weather.

'Tis beauty truly blent, whose red and white / Nature's own sweet and cunning hand laid on: / Lady, you are the cruel'st she alive, / If you will lead these graces to the grave, / And leave the world no copy.

It's true beauty, perfectly blended, whose red and white were laid on by nature's own sweet and skilful hand. Lady, you are the cruellest woman alive if you take these graces to the grave and leave the world no copy.

O, sir, I will not be so hard-hearted; I will give out / divers schedules of my beauty. It shall be inventoried; and every / particle and utensil labelled to my will: as, item, two lips / indifferent red; item, two grey eyes with lids to them; item, one / neck, one chin, and so forth. Were you sent hither to praise me?

Oh, sir, I won't be so hard-hearted. I'll issue various lists of my beauty. It will be catalogued, and every part and item labelled and added to my will, like: item, two lips, reasonably red; item, two grey eyes, with lids; item, one neck, one chin, and so on. Were you sent here to praise me?

I see you what you are: you are too proud; / But, if you were the devil, you are fair. / My lord and master loves you. O, such love / Could be but recompens'd though you were crown'd / The nonpareil of beauty!

I see what you are: you are too proud. But even if you were the devil, you are beautiful. My lord and master loves you. Oh, love like his could only be repaid even if you were crowned the greatest beauty without equal!
With adorations, fertile tears, / With groans that thunder love, with sighs of fire.
With worship, with endless tears, with groans that thunder love, with fiery sighs.

Your lord does know my mind; I cannot love him: / Yet I suppose him virtuous, know him noble, / Of great estate, of fresh and stainless youth; / In voices well divulged, free, learn'd, and valiant, / And, in dimension and the shape of nature, / A gracious person: but yet I cannot love him; / He might have took his answer long ago.

Your lord knows my mind; I cannot love him. Yet I believe he is virtuous, I know he is noble, very rich, young and pure; he is well spoken of, generous, learned and brave, and in his build and figure a gracious person. But still I cannot love him. He could have taken his answer long ago.
If I did love you in my master's flame, / With such a suffering, such a deadly life, / In your denial I would find no sense, / I would not understand it.
If I loved you with my master's passion, with such suffering, a life like dying, I would find no sense in your refusal; I would not understand it.

Make me a willow cabin at your gate, / And call upon my soul within the house; / Write loyal cantons of contemned love, / And sing them loud, even in the dead of night; / Holla your name to the reverberate hills, / And make the babbling gossip of the air / Cry out Olivia! O, you should not rest / Between the elements of air and earth, / But you should pity me.

I'd make myself a hut of willow branches at your gate and call out to my soul inside your house. I'd write faithful songs of rejected love and sing them loudly, even in the dead of night. I'd shout your name to the echoing hills and make the chattering echo in the air cry out 'Olivia!' Oh, you would get no rest anywhere between the air and the earth until you pitied me.
You might do much. What is your parentage?
You might achieve a lot. What is your family background?
Above my fortunes, yet my state is well: I am a gentleman.
Better than my present fortunes, but my position is good. I am a gentleman.

Get you to your lord; / I cannot love him: let him send no more; / Unless, perchance, you come to me again, / To tell me how he takes it. Fare you well: / I thank you for your pains: spend this for me.
Go back to your lord. I cannot love him; let him send no more messengers, unless, perhaps, you come to me again to tell me how he takes it. Goodbye. Thank you for your trouble; spend this for me.

I am no fee'd post, lady; keep your purse; / My master, not myself, lacks recompense. / Love make his heart of flint that you shall love; / And let your fervour, like my master's, be / Placed in contempt! Farewell, fair cruelty.

I'm no hired messenger, lady; keep your purse. It's my master, not me, who lacks a reward. May Love turn the heart of the man you love to stone, and may your passion, like my master's, be treated with contempt! Goodbye, beautiful cruelty.

What is your parentage? / 'Above my fortunes, yet my state is well: / I am a gentleman.'—I'll be sworn thou art; / Thy tongue, thy face, thy limbs, actions, and spirit, / Do give thee five-fold blazon. Not too fast:—soft, soft! / Unless the master were the man.—How now? / Even so quickly may one catch the plague? / Methinks I feel this youth's perfections / With an invisible and subtle stealth / To creep in at mine eyes. Well, let it be.— / What, ho, Malvolio!—

'What is your family background?' 'Better than my fortunes, but my position is good. I am a gentleman.' I'll swear you are. Your speech, your face, your body, your actions and your spirit all give you a fivefold coat of arms. Not so fast! Slowly, slowly! If only the master were the servant. What's this? Can someone catch the plague so quickly? I feel this young man's perfections creeping in at my eyes with invisible, subtle stealth. Well, let it be. Hey there, Malvolio!

Run after that same peevish messenger, / The county's man: he left this ring behind him, / Would I or not; tell him I'll none of it. / Desire him not to flatter with his lord, / Nor hold him up with hopes; I am not for him: / If that the youth will come this way to-morrow, / I'll give him reasons for't. Hie thee, Malvolio.

Run after that rude messenger, the Count's servant. He left this ring behind, whether I wanted it or not; tell him I'll have none of it. Tell him not to flatter his lord or keep his hopes up; I am not for him. If the youth will come this way tomorrow, I'll give him my reasons. Hurry, Malvolio.
I do I know not what: and fear to find / Mine eye too great a flatterer for my mind. / Fate, show thy force. Ourselves we do not owe: / What is decreed must be; and be this so!
I'm doing I don't know what, and I'm afraid my eyes have flattered my judgment. Fate, show your power. We don't own ourselves. What is destined must be, and let it be so!
Will you stay no longer; nor will you not that I go with you?
Won't you stay any longer, and won't you let me go with you?

By your patience, no; my stars shine darkly over me; the / malignancy of my fate might, perhaps, distemper yours; therefore / I shall crave of you your leave that I may bear my evils alone. / It were a bad recompense for your love, to lay any of them on / you.

With your permission, no. My stars shine darkly over me, and the evil of my fate might perhaps infect yours. So I must ask your leave to bear my troubles alone. It would be a poor reward for your love to put any of them on you.
Let me know of you whither you are bound.
At least tell me where you are going.

No, 'sooth, sir; my determinate voyage is mere / extravagancy. But I perceive in you so excellent a touch of / modesty, that you will not extort from me what I am willing to / keep in; therefore it charges me in manners the rather to express / myself. You must know of me then, Antonio, my name is Sebastian, / which I called Rodorigo; my father was that Sebastian of / Messaline whom I know you have heard of: he left behind him / myself and a sister, both born in an hour; if the heavens had / been pleased, would we had so ended! but you, sir, altered that; / for some hours before you took me from the breach of the sea was / my sister drowned.

No, honestly, sir; the journey I've decided on is just wandering. But I see in you such a fine touch of modesty that you won't force from me what I want to keep to myself; so good manners oblige me all the more to reveal myself. You must know, then, Antonio, that my name is Sebastian, though I called myself Roderigo. My father was that Sebastian of Messaline whom I know you have heard of. He left behind me and a sister, both born in the same hour. If heaven had been willing, I wish we had ended together too! But you, sir, changed that, because a few hours before you pulled me out of the breaking waves my sister was drowned.

A lady, sir, though it was said she much resembled me, / was yet of many accounted beautiful: but though I could not, with / such estimable wonder, overfar believe that, yet thus far I will / boldly publish her,—she bore mind that envy could not but call / fair. She is drowned already, sir, with salt water, though I seem / to drown her remembrance again with more.

She was a lady, sir, who was thought beautiful by many, although people said she looked very like me. Though I can't go so far as to believe such generous praise, I will boldly declare this much: she had a mind that even envy would have to call beautiful. She is drowned already, sir, in salt water, though I seem to drown her memory again with more.
Pardon me, sir, your bad entertainment.
Forgive me, sir, for the poor hospitality I've given you.
O, good Antonio, forgive me your trouble.
Oh, good Antonio, forgive me for all the trouble I've caused you.
If you will not murder me for my love, let me be your servant.
If you don't want to kill me for my love, let me be your servant.

If you will not undo what you have done—that is, kill / him whom you have recovered—desire it not. Fare ye well at once; / my bosom is full of kindness; and I am yet so near the manners of / my mother that, upon the least occasion more, mine eyes will tell / tales of me. I am bound to the Count Orsino's court: farewell.

If you don't want to undo what you've done, that is, kill the man you saved, don't ask it. Goodbye at once. My heart is full of feeling, and I'm still so close to my mother's ways that at the slightest further cause my eyes will give me away with tears. I am going to Count Orsino's court. Farewell.

The gentleness of all the gods go with thee! / I have many enemies in Orsino's court, / Else would I very shortly see thee there: / But come what may, I do adore thee so / That danger shall seem sport, and I will go.

May the kindness of all the gods go with you! I have many enemies in Orsino's court, or I would soon see you there. But whatever happens, I love you so much that danger will seem like a game, and I will go.
Were you not even now with the Countess Olivia?
Weren't you with the Countess Olivia just now?
Even now, sir; on a moderate pace I have since arrived but / hither.
Just now, sir; walking at a moderate pace, I've only got as far as here since.

She returns this ring to you, sir; you might have saved / me my pains, to have taken it away yourself. She adds moreover, / that you should put your lord into a desperate assurance she will / none of him: and one thing more: that you be never so hardy to / come again in his affairs, unless it be to report your lord's / taking of this. Receive it so.

She returns this ring to you, sir. You could have saved me the trouble by taking it away yourself. She adds that you should make your lord hopelessly certain that she will have nothing to do with him. And one thing more: that you should never be so bold as to come again on his business, unless it's to report how your lord takes this. Take it, then.
She took the ring of me: I'll none of it.
She took the ring from me. I won't have it.
Come, sir, you peevishly threw it to her; and her will is / it should be so returned. If it be worth stooping for, there it / lies in your eye; if not, be it his that finds it.
Come, sir, you threw it to her rudely, and she wants it returned the same way. If it's worth bending down for, there it lies in front of you; if not, let whoever finds it keep it.

I left no ring with her; what means this lady? / Fortune forbid my outside have not charm'd her! / She made good view of me; indeed, so much, / That methought her eyes had lost her tongue, / For she did speak in starts distractedly. / She loves me, sure: the cunning of her passion / Invites me in this churlish messenger. / None of my lord's ring! why, he sent her none. / I am the man; —if it be so,—as 'tis,— / Poor lady, she were better love a dream. / Disguise, I see thou art a wickedness / Wherein the pregnant enemy does much. / How easy is it for the proper-false / In women's waxen hearts to set their forms! / Alas, our frailty is the cause, not we; / For such as we are made of, such we be. / How will this fadge? My master loves her dearly, / And I, poor monster, fond as much on him; / And she, mistaken, seems to dote on me. / What will become of this? As I am man, / My state is desperate for my master's love; / As I am woman, now alas the day! / What thriftless sighs shall poor Olivia breathe! / O time, thou must untangle this, not I; / It is too hard a knot for me to untie!

I left no ring with her. What does this lady mean? Heaven forbid that my appearance has charmed her! She looked me over carefully; so carefully, in fact, that I thought her eyes had made her lose her tongue, because she spoke in broken, distracted bursts. She loves me, surely. The cunning of her passion invites me through this rude messenger. She'll have none of my lord's ring! Why, he sent her none. I am the man. If that's so, and it is, poor lady, she would do better to love a dream. Disguise, I see you are a wickedness that the cunning devil makes much use of. How easy it is for handsome deceivers to stamp their image on women's soft, wax-like hearts! Alas, our weakness is the cause, not we ourselves, for we are what we are made of. How will this work out? My master loves her dearly, and I, poor monster, love him just as much, and she, mistaken, seems to dote on me. What will become of this? As I am a man, I have no hope of my master's love; as I am a woman, alas the day, what useless sighs poor Olivia will breathe! Oh time, you must untangle this, not I. It is too hard a knot for me to untie!
Approach, Sir Andrew; not to be a-bed after midnight is to / be up betimes; and diluculo surgere, thou know'st.
Come here, Sir Andrew. Not to be in bed after midnight is to be up early; and 'to rise early is healthy', as you know.
Nay; by my troth, I know not; but I know to be up late / is to be up late.
No, honestly, I don't know; but I know that to be up late is to be up late.

A false conclusion; I hate it as an unfilled can. To be / up after midnight, and to go to bed then is early: so that to go / to bed after midnight is to go to bed betimes. Do not our lives / consist of the four elements?

A false conclusion; I hate it as much as an empty mug. To be up after midnight and go to bed then is early, so going to bed after midnight is going to bed early. Aren't our lives made up of the four elements?
Faith, so they say; but I think it rather consists of / eating and drinking.
Honestly, so they say; but I think life is made up of eating and drinking.
Thou art a scholar; let us therefore eat and drink.— / Marian, I say!—a stoup of wine.
You're a scholar; so let's eat and drink. Marian, I say! A jug of wine!
Here comes the fool, i' faith.
How now, my hearts? Did you never see the picture of we three?
Hello, my hearties! Haven't you ever seen the picture of 'we three'?
Welcome, ass. Now let's have a catch.
Welcome, ass. Now let's have a round song.

By my troth, the fool has an excellent breast. I had / rather than forty shillings I had such a leg; and so sweet a / breath to sing, as the fool has. In sooth, thou wast in very / gracious fooling last night when thou spokest of Pigrogromitus, / of the Vapians passing the equinoctial of Queubus; 'twas very / good, i' faith. I sent thee sixpence for thy leman. Hadst it?

Honestly, the fool has an excellent voice. I'd give forty shillings to have such a leg for dancing, and such a sweet voice for singing, as the fool has. Truly, you were fooling beautifully last night when you talked about Pigrogromitus, and the Vapians crossing the equator of Queubus. It was very good, honestly. I sent you sixpence for your sweetheart. Did you get it?
I did impeticos thy gratillity; for Malvolio's nose is no / whipstock. My lady has a white hand, and the Myrmidons are no / bottle-ale houses.
I pocketed your little tip; for Malvolio's nose is no whip handle, my lady has a white hand, and the Myrmidons are no cheap beer houses.
Excellent! Why, this is the best fooling, when all is / done. Now, a song.
Excellent! Why, this is the best fooling, when all's said and done. Now, a song.
Come on; there is sixpence for you: let's have a song.
Come on, there's sixpence for you. Let's have a song.
There's a testril of me too: if one knight give a—
There's a sixpence from me too. If one knight gives a...
Would you have a love-song, or a song of good life?
Would you like a love song, or a song about living well?
A love song, a love song.
Ay, ay; I care not for good life.
Yes, yes, I don't care for living well.

O, mistress mine, where are you roaming? / O, stay and hear; your true love's coming, / That can sing both high and low: / Trip no further, pretty sweeting; / Journeys end in lovers meeting, / Every wise man's son doth know.

Oh my mistress, where are you wandering? Oh, stay and listen; your true love is coming, who can sing both high and low. Don't run any further, pretty sweetheart. Journeys end when lovers meet, as every wise man's son knows.

What is love? 'tis not hereafter; / Present mirth hath present laughter; / What's to come is still unsure. / In delay there lies no plenty; / Then come kiss me, sweet and twenty; / Youth's a stuff will not endure.

What is love? It isn't in the future. Present happiness brings present laughter; what's to come is always uncertain. There's nothing to be gained by delay. So come and kiss me, sweet one, twenty times over. Youth is a thing that won't last.
A mellifluous voice, as I am true knight.
A honey-sweet voice, as I'm a true knight.
Very sweet and contagious, i' faith.

To hear by the nose, it is dulcet in contagion. But shall / we make the welkin dance indeed? Shall we rouse the night-owl in / a catch that will draw three souls out of one weaver? shall we do / that?
If we heard through our noses, it would be a sweet disease. But shall we make the sky dance? Shall we wake the owl with a round song that would draw three souls out of a weaver? Shall we do that?
An you love me, let's do't: I am dog at a catch.
If you love me, let's do it. I'm a real dog at a catch.
By'r lady, sir, and some dogs will catch well.
By Our Lady, sir, and some dogs catch well.
Most certain: let our catch be, 'Thou knave.'
Absolutely. Let our song be 'You knave'.
'Hold thy peace, thou knave' knight? I shall be constrain'd / in't to call thee knave, knight.
'Hold your peace, you knave', knight? Then I'll be forced to call you knave in it, knight.
'Tis not the first time I have constrained one to call / me knave. Begin, fool; it begins 'Hold thy peace.'
It's not the first time I've forced someone to call me knave. Begin, fool; it begins 'Hold your peace'.
I shall never begin if I hold my peace.
I'll never begin if I hold my peace.
What a caterwauling do you keep here! If my lady have not / called up her steward Malvolio, and bid him turn you out of / doors, never trust me.
What a racket you're making in here! If my lady hasn't called her steward Malvolio and told him to throw you out, never trust me again.

My lady's a Cataian, we are politicians; Malvolio's a / Peg-a-Ramsey, and / [Singing.] / 'Three merry men be we.' / Am not I consanguineous? am I not of her blood? Tilly-valley, / lady. / 'There dwelt a man in Babylon, lady, lady.'

My lady's a Chinese trickster, we are schemers, Malvolio's a killjoy, and [Singing] 'Three merry men are we.' Aren't I related to her? Am I not of her blood? Nonsense, lady! [Singing] 'There lived a man in Babylon, lady, lady.'
Beshrew me, the knight's in admirable fooling.
Curse me, the knight is fooling wonderfully.
Ay, he does well enough if he be disposed, and so do I / too; he does it with a better grace, but I do it more natural.
Yes, he does well enough when he's in the mood, and so do I. He does it more gracefully, but I do it more naturally.
[Singing] O, the twelfth day of December,—
[Singing] Oh, on the twelfth day of December...
For the love o' God, peace!
For the love of God, quiet!

My masters, are you mad? or what are you? Have you no / wit, manners, nor honesty, but to gabble like tinkers at this / time of night? Do ye make an ale-house of my lady's house, that / ye squeak out your coziers' catches without any mitigation or / remorse of voice? Is there no respect of place, persons, nor / time, in you?

Gentlemen, are you mad, or what are you? Have you no sense, manners or decency, that you gabble like tinkers at this time of night? Are you turning my lady's house into a pub, that you screech your cobblers' songs without any softening of your voices? Have you no respect for the place, the people or the time?
We did keep time, sir, in our catches. Sneck up!
We kept time, sir, in our songs. Get lost!

Sir Toby, I must be round with you. My lady bade me tell / you that, though she harbours you as her kinsman she's nothing / allied to your disorders. If you can separate yourself and your / misdemeanours, you are welcome to the house; if not, an it would / please you to take leave of her, she is very willing to bid you / farewell.

Sir Toby, I must be blunt with you. My lady told me to tell you that although she gives you a home as her relative, she wants nothing to do with your disorderly behaviour. If you can separate yourself from your misbehaviour, you are welcome in the house. If not, and you would like to leave her, she is very willing to say goodbye to you.
'Farewell, dear heart, since I must needs be gone.'
[Singing] 'Farewell, dear heart, since I must needs be gone.'
'His eyes do show his days are almost done.'
[Singing] 'His eyes do show his days are almost done.'
This is much credit to you.
'Shall I bid him go, and spare not?'
[Singing] 'Shall I tell him to go, and not spare him?'
'O, no, no, no, no, you dare not.'
[Singing] 'Oh no, no, no, no, you don't dare.'
Out o' tune? sir, ye lie. Art any more than a steward? Dost thou / think, because thou art virtuous, there shall be no more cakes / and ale?
Out of tune, sir? You lie. Are you anything more than a steward? Do you think that because you are virtuous there will be no more cakes and ale?
Yes, by Saint Anne; and ginger shall be hot i' the mouth / too.
Yes, by Saint Anne, and ginger will still be hot in the mouth too.
Thou'art i' the right.—Go, sir, rub your chain with crumbs: / A stoup of wine, Maria!
You're right. Go, sir, polish your steward's chain with breadcrumbs. A jug of wine, Maria!
Mistress Mary, if you prized my lady's favour at anything / more than contempt, you would not give means for this uncivil / rule; she shall know of it, by this hand.
Mistress Mary, if you valued my lady's favour at anything more than contempt, you wouldn't help this unruly behaviour. She will hear of it, by this hand.
Go and waggle your ears like the donkey you are.
'Twere as good a deed as to drink when a man's a-hungry, / to challenge him the field, and then to break promise with him / and make a fool of him.
It would be as good a deed as drinking when you're hungry to challenge him to a duel, then not turn up and make a fool of him.
Do't, knight; I'll write thee a challenge; or I'll / deliver thy indignation to him by word of mouth.
Do it, knight. I'll write you a challenge, or I'll deliver your anger to him in person.

Sweet Sir Toby, be patient for to-night; since the youth of / the count's was to-day with my lady, she is much out of quiet. / For Monsieur Malvolio, let me alone with him: if I do not gull / him into a nayword, and make him a common recreation, do not / think I have wit enough to lie straight in my bed. I know I can / do it.

Sweet Sir Toby, be patient tonight. Since the Count's young man was with my lady today, she has been very unsettled. As for Monsieur Malvolio, leave him to me. If I don't trick him into becoming a byword and make him a public joke, don't think I have the sense to lie straight in my bed. I know I can do it.
Possess us, possess us; tell us something of him.
Tell us, tell us; tell us something about him.
Marry, sir, sometimes he is a kind of Puritan.
Well, sir, sometimes he is a kind of Puritan.
O, if I thought that, I'd beat him like a dog.
Oh, if I thought that, I'd beat him like a dog.
What, for being a Puritan? thy exquisite reason, dear knight?
What, for being a Puritan? Your excellent reason, dear knight?
I have no exquisite reason for't, but I have reason good enough.
I don't have an excellent reason for it, but I have a good enough reason.

The devil a Puritan that he is, or anything constantly but a / time-pleaser: an affectioned ass that cons state without book and / utters it by great swarths; the best persuaded of himself, so / crammed, as he thinks, with excellences, that it is his grounds / of faith that all that look on him love him; and on that vice in / him will my revenge find notable cause to work.

He's no more a Puritan than the devil is, or anything else consistently, except someone who bends with the times. He's an affected ass who learns grand phrases by heart and pours them out in great swathes. He thinks so well of himself, so crammed, as he believes, with good qualities, that it's an article of faith with him that everyone who looks at him loves him. And that's the vice in him my revenge will use to great effect.

I will drop in his way some obscure epistles of love; / wherein, by the colour of his beard, the shape of his leg, the / manner of his gait, the expressure of his eye, forehead, and / complexion, he shall find himself most feelingly personated. I / can write very like my lady, your niece; on a forgotten matter we / can hardly make distinction of our hands.

I'll drop some mysterious love letters in his path. In them he'll find himself described in the most touching detail: the colour of his beard, the shape of his leg, the way he walks, the look of his eyes, his forehead and complexion. I can write very like my lady, your niece; when we look at something written long ago, we can hardly tell our handwriting apart.
I have't in my nose too.
I've got it in my nose too.
He shall think, by the letters that thou wilt drop, that / they come from my niece, and that she is in love with him.
From the letters you drop, he'll think they come from my niece, and that she's in love with him.
My purpose is, indeed, a horse of that colour.
That's exactly the colour of horse I'm riding.
And your horse now would make him an ass.
And your horse would make him an ass.

Sport royal, I warrant you. I know my physic will work with / him. I will plant you two, and let the fool make a third, where / he shall find the letter; observe his construction of it. For / this night, to bed, and dream on the event. Farewell.

Royal entertainment, I promise you. I know my medicine will work on him. I'll hide you two, and the fool can make a third, where he'll find the letter. Watch how he interprets it. For tonight, go to bed and dream about what will happen. Goodbye.
Before me, she's a good wench.
Upon my soul, she's a good girl.
She's a beagle true bred, and one that adores me. What o' that?
She's a true-bred beagle, and she adores me. What of it?
Let's to bed, knight.—Thou hadst need send for more money.
Let's go to bed, knight. You'll need to send for more money.
If I cannot recover your niece I am a foul way out.
If I can't win your niece, I'm badly out of pocket.
Send for money, knight; if thou hast her not i' the end, / call me Cut.
Send for money, knight. If you don't get her in the end, call me a nag.
If I do not, never trust me; take it how you will.
If I don't, never trust me, take it how you like.
Come, come; I'll go burn some sack; 'tis too late to go / to bed now: come, knight; come, knight.
Come on, come on, I'll go and warm some sherry. It's too late to go to bed now. Come on, knight; come on, knight.

Give me some music:—Now, good morrow, friends:— / Now, good Cesario, but that piece of song, / That old and antique song we heard last night; / Methought it did relieve my passion much; / More than light airs and recollected terms / Of these most brisk and giddy-paced times:— / Come, but one verse.

Give me some music. Good morning, friends. Now, good Cesario, just that bit of song, that old-fashioned song we heard last night. I thought it eased my feelings a great deal, more than the light tunes and studied phrases of these lively, fast-moving times. Come, just one verse.
He is not here, so please your lordship, that should sing it.
If it please your lordship, the man who should sing it isn't here.
Feste, the jester, my lord; a fool that the Lady Olivia's / father took much delight in: he is about the house.
Feste the jester, my lord, a fool that Lady Olivia's father was very fond of. He's somewhere about the house.
Seek him out, and play the tune the while.
Find him, and play the tune meanwhile.

Come hither, boy. If ever thou shalt love, / In the sweet pangs of it remember me: / For, such as I am, all true lovers are; / Unstaid and skittish in all motions else, / Save in the constant image of the creature / That is belov'd.—How dost thou like this tune?

Come here, boy. If you ever fall in love, remember me in its sweet pains. For all true lovers are like me: unsettled and restless in every feeling except the constant image of the one they love. How do you like this tune?
It gives a very echo to the seat / Where Love is throned.
It echoes the very place where Love sits enthroned.
Thou dost speak masterly: / My life upon't, young though thou art, thine eye / Hath stayed upon some favour that it loves; / Hath it not, boy?
You speak like a master. I'd bet my life that, young as you are, your eye has rested on some face it loves. Hasn't it, boy?
A little, if you'll allow it.
What kind of woman is she?
She is not worth thee, then. What years, i' faith?
Then she isn't worthy of you. How old, honestly?

Too old, by heaven! Let still the woman take / An elder than herself; so wears she to him, / So sways she level in her husband's heart. / For, boy, however we do praise ourselves, / Our fancies are more giddy and unfirm, / More longing, wavering, sooner lost and won, / Than women's are.

Too old, by heaven! A woman should always take someone older than herself. That way she adapts to him and keeps a steady place in her husband's heart. For, boy, however we praise ourselves, our affections are more giddy and unsteady, more full of longing and wavering, sooner lost and won, than women's are.
I think it well, my lord.
Then let thy love be younger than thyself, / Or thy affection cannot hold the bent: / For women are as roses, whose fair flower, / Being once display'd, doth fall that very hour.
Then let your love be younger than you, or your affection can't stay at full stretch. For women are like roses: once their lovely flower has opened, it falls that very hour.
And so they are: alas, that they are so; / To die, even when they to perfection grow!
And so they are. Alas, that they are like that: to die just when they grow to perfection!

O, fellow, come, the song we had last night:— / Mark it, Cesario; it is old and plain: / The spinsters and the knitters in the sun, / And the free maids, that weave their thread with bones, / Do use to chant it: it is silly sooth, / And dallies with the innocence of love / Like the old age.

Oh, fellow, come, the song we had last night. Listen to it, Cesario; it is old and simple. The women spinning and knitting in the sun, and the carefree girls weaving lace with bone bobbins, often sing it. It's plain truth, and it plays with the innocence of love like the good old days.

Come away, come away, death. / And in sad cypress let me be laid; / Fly away, fly away, breath; / I am slain by a fair cruel maid. / My shroud of white, stuck all with yew, / O, prepare it! / My part of death no one so true / Did share it. / Not a flower, not a flower sweet, / On my black coffin let there be strown: / Not a friend, not a friend greet / My poor corpse where my bones shall be thrown: / A thousand thousand sighs to save, / Lay me, O, where / Sad true lover never find my grave, / To weep there!

Come away, come away, death, and let me be laid in a sad coffin of cypress. Fly away, fly away, breath; I am killed by a beautiful, cruel girl. My white shroud, decorated all over with yew, oh, prepare it! No one so faithful ever played his part in death as I do. Let not a flower, not a sweet flower, be scattered on my black coffin. Let not a friend, not a friend greet my poor body where my bones are thrown. To save a thousand thousand sighs, lay me, oh, where no sad true lover can find my grave to weep there!
No pains, sir; I take pleasure in singing, sir.
No pains, sir. I take pleasure in singing, sir.
Then I'll pay for your pleasure.
Truly, sir, and pleasure will be paid one time or another.
Truly, sir, pleasure has to be paid for sooner or later.
Give me now leave to leave thee.
Allow me now to dismiss you.

Now the melancholy god protect thee; and the tailor make thy / doublet of changeable taffeta, for thy mind is a very opal!—I / would have men of such constancy put to sea, that their business / might be everything, and their intent everywhere; for that's it / that always makes a good voyage of nothing.—Farewell.

Now may the god of melancholy protect you, and may the tailor make your jacket of shot silk that changes colour, because your mind is a real opal! I'd like men as constant as you to be sent to sea, where their business could be anything and their destination anywhere, because that's how you make a good voyage out of nothing. Goodbye.
Let all the rest give place.—
Let all the rest of you leave.

Once more, Cesario, / Get thee to yond same sovereign cruelty: / Tell her my love, more noble than the world, / Prizes not quantity of dirty lands; / The parts that fortune hath bestow'd upon her, / Tell her, I hold as giddily as fortune; / But 'tis that miracle and queen of gems / That Nature pranks her in attracts my soul.

Once more, Cesario, go to that queen of cruelty. Tell her my love, which is nobler than the world, doesn't value quantities of muddy land. Tell her I regard the wealth that fortune has given her as lightly as fortune itself does. It is the miracle, that queen of jewels, her beauty, with which Nature has adorned her, that draws my soul.
But if she cannot love you, sir?
But what if she cannot love you, sir?

'Sooth, but you must. / Say that some lady, as perhaps there is, / Hath for your love as great a pang of heart / As you have for Olivia: you cannot love her; / You tell her so. Must she not then be answer'd?

Truly, you must. Suppose some lady, as perhaps there is, feels as great a pain in her heart for love of you as you feel for Olivia. You cannot love her; you tell her so. Mustn't she accept that answer?

There is no woman's sides / Can bide the beating of so strong a passion / As love doth give my heart: no woman's heart / So big to hold so much; they lack retention. / Alas, their love may be called appetite,— / No motion of the liver, but the palate,— / That suffer surfeit, cloyment, and revolt; / But mine is all as hungry as the sea, / And can digest as much: make no compare / Between that love a woman can bear me / And that I owe Olivia.

No woman's body could withstand the beating of such a strong passion as love gives my heart. No woman's heart is big enough to hold so much; they can't hold on to it. Alas, their love could be called appetite, a craving not of the liver, the seat of passion, but of the tongue, which gets overfed, sick of it, and disgusted. But mine is as hungry as the sea and can digest as much. Don't compare the love a woman could feel for me with the love I have for Olivia.
Too well what love women to men may owe. / In faith, they are as true of heart as we. / My father had a daughter loved a man, / As it might be perhaps, were I a woman, / I should your lordship.
Only too well what love women can feel for men. Truly, they are as faithful in heart as we are. My father had a daughter who loved a man, as I might perhaps love your lordship, if I were a woman.

A blank, my lord. She never told her love, / But let concealment, like a worm i' the bud, / Feed on her damask cheek: she pined in thought; / And with a green and yellow melancholy, / She sat like patience on a monument, / Smiling at grief. Was not this love, indeed? / We men may say more, swear more; but indeed, / Our shows are more than will; for still we prove / Much in our vows, but little in our love.

A blank page, my lord. She never told of her love, but let the secret, like a worm in the bud, feed on her rose-pink cheek. She pined away in thought, and with a pale, sickly sadness she sat like a statue of Patience on a tomb, smiling at grief. Wasn't this love indeed? We men may say more and swear more, but really our displays are greater than our feelings, because we always turn out to be strong in our vows but weak in our love.
But died thy sister of her love, my boy?
But did your sister die of her love, my boy?
I am all the daughters of my father's house, / And all the brothers too;—and yet I know not.— / Sir, shall I to this lady?
I am all the daughters of my father's house, and all the brothers too, and yet I don't know. Sir, shall I go to this lady?
Ay, that's the theme. / To her in haste: give her this jewel; say / My love can give no place, bide no denay.
Yes, that's the point. Go to her quickly. Give her this jewel, and say my love will not give way or accept a refusal.
Nay, I'll come; if I lose a scruple of this sport let me be / boiled to death with melancholy.
Oh, I'll come. If I miss a scrap of this fun, let me be boiled to death in melancholy.
Wouldst thou not be glad to have the niggardly rascally / sheep-biter come by some notable shame?
Wouldn't you be glad to see the stingy, rascally, sneaking dog brought to some great shame?
I would exult, man; you know he brought me out o' favour / with my lady about a bear-baiting here.
I'd be overjoyed, man. You know he got me into trouble with my lady over a bear-baiting here.
To anger him we'll have the bear again; and we will fool / him black and blue:—shall we not, Sir Andrew?
To make him angry, we'll bring the bear back again, and we'll make a fool of him till he's black and blue. Won't we, Sir Andrew?
An we do not, it is pity of our lives.
If we don't, it'll be a shame on our lives.
Here comes the little villain:—How now, my nettle of India?
Here comes the little villain. Well now, my golden treasure?

Get ye all three into the box-tree: Malvolio's coming down / this walk; he has been yonder i' the sun practising behaviour to / his own shadow this half hour: observe him, for the love of / mockery; for I know this letter will make a contemplative idiot / of him. Close, in the name of jesting! [The men hide themselves.] / Lie thou there; [Throws down a letter] for here comes the trout / that must be caught with tickling.

Get into the box hedge, all three of you. Malvolio's coming down this path. He's been over there in the sun for the last half hour practising his manners to his own shadow. Watch him, for the love of mockery, because I know this letter will make a daydreaming idiot of him. Hide, in the name of fun! [The men hide] You lie there [She drops a letter], because here comes the trout that must be caught by tickling.
