'Tis but fortune; all is fortune. Maria once told me she / did affect me: and I have heard herself come thus near, that, / should she fancy, it should be one of my complexion. Besides, she / uses me with a more exalted respect than any one else that / follows her. What should I think on't?

It's all luck; everything is luck. Maria once told me that she liked me, and I've heard my lady herself come close to saying that, if she ever fell in love, it would be with someone of my type. Besides, she treats me with more respect than anyone else who serves her. What should I make of that?
O, peace! Contemplation makes a rare turkey-cock of him; / how he jets under his advanced plumes!
Oh, quiet! Daydreaming makes a splendid turkey-cock of him. Look how he struts with his feathers spread!
'Slight, I could so beat the rogue:—
By God's light, I could beat the rogue...
There is example for't; the lady of the Strachy married / the yeoman of the wardrobe.
There's a precedent for it: the Lady of Strachy married the servant in charge of her wardrobe.
O, peace! now he's deeply in; look how imagination blows him.
Oh, quiet! Now he's deep in it. Look how his imagination puffs him up.
Having been three months married to her, sitting in my state,—
After three months of marriage to her, sitting in my chair of state...
O for a stone-bow to hit him in the eye!
Oh, for a catapult to hit him in the eye!
Calling my officers about me, in my branched velvet gown; / having come from a day-bed, where I have left Olivia sleeping.
Calling my officers around me, in my embroidered velvet gown, having come from a couch where I've left Olivia sleeping...
And then to have the humour of state: and after a demure / travel of regard,—telling them I know my place as I would they / should do theirs,—to ask for my kinsman Toby.
And then to adopt the mood of a great man, and after a serious glance around the room, telling them I know my place as I want them to know theirs, to ask for my relative Toby...
O, peace, peace, peace! Now, now.
Oh, quiet, quiet, quiet! Now, now.
Seven of my people, with an obedient start, make out for / him: I frown the while, and perchance, wind up my watch, or play / with some rich jewel. Toby approaches; court'sies there to me:
Seven of my servants, jumping to obey, go out to fetch him. I frown meanwhile, and perhaps wind up my watch, or play with some rich jewel. Toby comes in and bows to me there...
Shall this fellow be allowed to live?
Though our silence be drawn from us with cars, yet peace.
Even if our silence is dragged out of us with carts, keep quiet.
I extend my hand to him thus, quenching my familiar smile with an / austere regard of control:
I hold out my hand to him like this, cooling my friendly smile with a stern look of authority...
And does not Toby take you a blow o' the lips then?
And doesn't Toby give you a punch on the mouth then?
Saying 'Cousin Toby, my fortunes having cast me on your / niece, give me this prerogative of speech':—
Saying, 'Cousin Toby, since my good fortune has given me your niece, allow me the right to say this...'
Nay, patience, or we break the sinews of our plot.
No, be patient, or we'll cut the sinews of our plot.
'Besides, you waste the treasure of your time with a / foolish knight';
'Besides, you waste the treasure of your time with a foolish knight...'
I knew 'twas I; for many do call me fool.
I knew it was me, because many people call me a fool.
What business do we have here?
Now is the woodcock near the gin.
Now the stupid bird is near the trap.
O, peace! And the spirit of humours intimate reading aloud to / him!
Oh, quiet! And may the spirit of whims make him read it out loud!
By my life, this is my lady's hand: these be her very / C's, her U's, and her T's; and thus makes she her great P's. It / is in contempt of question, her hand.
Upon my life, this is my lady's handwriting. These are her very C's, her U's and her T's, and this is how she makes her capital P's. It's her handwriting beyond any question.
Her C's, her U's, and her T's. Why that?
Her C's, her U's and her T's. Why that?

[Reads] 'To the unknown beloved, this, and my good / wishes.' Her very phrases!—By your leave, wax.—Soft!—and the / impressure her Lucrece, with which she uses to seal: 'tis my / lady. To whom should this be?

[Reads] 'To the unknown beloved, this, and my good wishes.' Her very phrases! Excuse me, wax. Wait! And the seal is her Lucrece, which she always uses to seal her letters. It's my lady. Who can this be for?
This wins him, liver and all.
This will win him over completely, liver and all.
[Reads] / 'Jove knows I love, / But who? / Lips, do not move, / No man must know.' / 'No man must know.'—What follows? the numbers alter'd!—'No man / must know':—If this should be thee, Malvolio?
[Reads] 'Jove knows I love, but who? Lips, do not move; no man must know.' 'No man must know.' What comes next? The metre changes! 'No man must know.' What if this were you, Malvolio?
'I may command where I adore: / But silence, like a Lucrece knife, / With bloodless stroke my heart doth gore; / M, O, A, I, doth sway my life.'
[Reads] 'I may command where I adore, but silence, like Lucrece's knife, stabs my heart with a bloodless blow. M.O.A.I. rules my life.'
'M, O, A, I, doth sway my life.'—Nay, but first let me see,—let / me see,—let me see.
'M.O.A.I. rules my life.' No, but first let me see, let me see, let me see.
What dish of poison has she dressed him!
What a dish of poison she has prepared for him!
And with what wing the stannyel checks at it!
And how quickly the hawk swoops at it!

'I may command where I adore.' Why, she may command me: I / serve her, she is my lady. Why, this is evident to any formal / capacity; there is no obstruction in this;—And the end,—What / should that alphabetical position portend? If I could make that / resemble something in me.—Softly!—M, O, A, I.—

'I may command where I adore.' Why, she can command me; I serve her, she is my lady. Why, this is obvious to any normal intelligence; there's no difficulty in this. And the end: what could that arrangement of letters mean? If I could make that resemble something in me. Gently! M.O.A.I.
O, ay, make up that:—he is now at a cold scent.
Oh yes, work that out. He's lost the scent now.
Sowter will cry upon't for all this, though it be as rank as a / fox.
The hound will still bark at it, though it stinks as strongly as a fox.
M,—Malvolio; M,—why, that begins my name.
M: Malvolio. M: why, that's the first letter of my name.
Did not I say he would work it out? / The cur is excellent at faults.
Didn't I say he'd work it out? The dog is excellent at following a false trail.
M,—But then there is no consonancy in the sequel; that / suffers under probation: A should follow, but O does.
M. But then the rest doesn't fit; that fails when tested. A should come next, but O does.
And O shall end, I hope.
And O will end it, I hope.
Ay, or I'll cudgel him, and make him cry 'O!'
Yes, or I'll beat him and make him cry 'Oh!'
Ay, an you had any eye behind you, you might see more / detraction at your heels than fortunes before you.
Yes, and if you had an eye behind you, you'd see more disgrace at your heels than good fortune in front of you.

M, O, A, I;—This simulation is not as the former:—and / yet, to crush this a little, it would bow to me, for every one of / these letters are in my name. Soft; here follows prose.— / 'If this fall into thy hand, revolve. In my stars I am above / thee; but be not afraid of greatness. Some are born great, some / achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon them. Thy / fates open their hands; let thy blood and spirit embrace them. / And, to inure thyself to what thou art like to be, cast thy / humble slough and appear fresh. Be opposite with a kinsman, surly / with servants: let thy tongue tang arguments of state; put / thyself into the trick of singularity: She thus advises thee that / sighs for thee. Remember who commended thy yellow stockings, and / wished to see thee ever cross-gartered. I say, remember. Go to; / thou art made, if thou desirest to be so; if not, let me see thee / a steward still, the fellow of servants, and not worthy to touch / fortune's fingers. Farewell. She that would alter services with / thee, / 'The fortunate-unhappy.' / Daylight and champian discovers not more: this is open. I will be / proud, I will read politic authors, I will baffle Sir Toby, I / will wash off gross acquaintance, I will be point-device, the / very man. I do not now fool myself to let imagination jade me; / for every reason excites to this, that my lady loves me. She did / commend my yellow stockings of late, she did praise my leg being / cross-gartered; and in this she manifests herself to my love, and / with a kind of injunction, drives me to these habits of her / liking. I thank my stars I am happy. I will be strange, stout, in / yellow stockings, and cross-gartered, even with the swiftness of / putting on. Jove and my stars be praised!—Here is yet a / postscript. 'Thou canst not choose but know who I am. If thou / entertainest my love, let it appear in thy smiling; thy smiles / become thee well: therefore in my presence still smile, dear my / sweet, I pr'ythee.' Jove, I thank thee. I will smile; I will do / everything that thou wilt have me.

M.O.A.I. This disguise isn't as clear as the earlier part; and yet, if I squeeze it a little, it would bend to fit me, because every one of these letters is in my name. Wait, here comes some prose. [Reads] 'If this falls into your hands, think it over. My stars place me above you, but don't be afraid of greatness. Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon them. Your fates are holding out their hands; let your courage and spirit embrace them. And to get used to what you are likely to become, throw off your humble skin and appear new. Be hostile to a relative and rude to servants; let your tongue ring out political arguments, and adopt the habit of being different. This is the advice of the one who sighs for you. Remember who praised your yellow stockings and wanted always to see you with your garters crossed. I say, remember. Go on, your fortune is made if you want it to be; if not, let me see you a steward still, the companion of servants, and not worthy to touch Fortune's fingers. Goodbye. She who would change places with you, The Fortunate-Unhappy.' Broad daylight and open country couldn't show more; this is clear. I will be proud, I will read political writers, I will humiliate Sir Toby, I will drop my low acquaintances, I will be perfect in every detail, exactly the man described. I'm not fooling myself now, letting my imagination trick me, because every reason points to this: my lady loves me. She did praise my yellow stockings recently, she did praise my leg in cross-garters, and in this she reveals her love for me, and with a kind of command urges me to dress the way she likes. I thank my stars I'm fortunate. I will be distant and haughty, in yellow stockings and cross-gartered, as fast as I can put them on. Jove and my stars be praised! Here's a postscript too. [Reads] 'You must know who I am. If you accept my love, let it show in your smiling; your smiles suit you well. So always smile in my presence, my dear sweet, I beg you.' Jove, I thank you. I will smile; I will do everything you want me to.
I will not give my part of this sport for a pension of / thousands to be paid from the Sophy.
I wouldn't give up my share of this fun for a pension of thousands paid by the Shah of Persia.
I could marry this wench for this device:
I could marry this girl for this trick.
And ask no other dowry with her but such another jest.
And ask for no other dowry with her than another joke like this.
Wilt thou set thy foot o' my neck?
Will you put your foot on my neck?
Shall I play my freedom at tray-trip, and become thy bond-slave?
Shall I gamble my freedom at dice and become your slave?
Why, thou hast put him in such a dream, that, when the / image of it leaves him, he must run mad.
Why, you've put him into such a dream that when the vision leaves him he'll go mad.
Nay, but say true; does it work upon him?
No, but tell me truly, is it working on him?

If you will then see the fruits of the sport, mark his / first approach before my lady: he will come to her in yellow / stockings, and 'tis a colour she abhors, and cross-gartered, a / fashion she detests; and he will smile upon her, which will now / be so unsuitable to her disposition, being addicted to a / melancholy as she is, that it cannot but turn him into a notable / contempt; if you will see it, follow me.

If you want to see the results of the joke, then watch how he first approaches my lady. He'll come to her in yellow stockings, a colour she hates, and cross-gartered, a fashion she detests. And he'll smile at her, which will be so out of keeping with her mood, given over to melancholy as she is, that it's bound to make him a figure of contempt. If you want to see it, follow me.
To the gates of Tartar, thou most excellent devil of wit!
To the gates of hell, you most excellent devil of wit!
Save thee, friend, and thy music. Dost thou live by thy tabor?
God save you, friend, and your music. Do you make your living by your drum?
No, sir, I live by the church.
No, sir, I live by the church.
No such matter, sir: I do live by the church; for I do live / at my house, and my house doth stand by the church.
Nothing like that, sir. I live by the church, because I live at my house, and my house stands by the church.
So thou mayst say the king lies by a beggar, if a beggar / dwell near him; or the church stands by thy tabor, if thy tabor / stand by the church.
In that case you could say the king lies with a beggar, if a beggar lives near him; or that the church stands by your drum, if your drum stands by the church.
You have said, sir.—To see this age!—A sentence is but a / cheveril glove to a good wit. How quickly the wrong side may be / turned outward!
You've said it, sir. What an age we live in! A sentence is just a soft kid glove to a clever wit. How quickly it can be turned inside out!
Nay, that's certain; they that dally nicely with words may / quickly make them wanton.
Yes, that's certain. People who play cleverly with words can quickly make them loose.
I would, therefore, my sister had had no name, sir.
Then I wish my sister had had no name, sir.
Why, sir, her name's a word; and to dally with that word / might make my sister wanton. But indeed words are very rascals, / since bonds disgraced them.
Why, sir, her name's a word, and playing with that word might make my sister loose. But really, words have become complete rascals since people needed written contracts to be trusted.
Troth, sir, I can yield you none without words; and words / are grown so false I am loath to prove reason with them.
Honestly, sir, I can't give you one without words, and words have become so false that I hate to prove anything with them.
I warrant, thou art a merry fellow, and carest for nothing.
I'm sure you're a cheerful fellow who cares about nothing.
Not so, sir, I do care for something: but in my conscience, / sir, I do not care for you; if that be to care for nothing, sir, / I would it would make you invisible.
Not so, sir, I do care about something. But honestly, sir, I don't care about you; and if that means caring about nothing, sir, I wish it would make you invisible.
Art not thou the Lady Olivia's fool?

No, indeed, sir; the Lady Olivia has no folly: she will keep / no fool, sir, till she be married; and fools are as like husbands / as pilchards are to herrings, the husband's the bigger; I am, / indeed, not her fool, but her corrupter of words.

No, indeed, sir. Lady Olivia has no foolishness. She won't keep a fool, sir, until she's married; and fools are as like husbands as sardines are like herrings: the husband's the bigger. I'm not really her fool, but her twister of words.
I saw thee late at the Count Orsino's.
I saw you recently at Count Orsino's.

Foolery, sir, does walk about the orb like the sun; it / shines everywhere. I would be sorry, sir, but the fool should be / as oft with your master as with my mistress: I think I saw your / wisdom there.
Foolery, sir, walks around the world like the sun; it shines everywhere. I'd be sorry, sir, if the fool weren't with your master as often as with my mistress. I think I saw your wise self there.
Nay, an thou pass upon me, I'll no more with thee. / Hold, there's expenses for thee.
No, if you're going to make fun of me, I'll have no more to do with you. Wait, here's something for your expenses.
Now Jove, in his next commodity of hair, send thee a beard!
Now may Jove, the next time he's handing out hair, send you a beard!
By my troth, I'll tell thee, I am almost sick for one; though I / would not have it grow on my chin. Is thy lady within?
Honestly, I'll tell you, I'm almost sick with longing for one, though I wouldn't want it to grow on my chin. Is your lady in?
Would not a pair of these have bred, sir?
Wouldn't a pair of these coins have bred, sir?
Yes, being kept together and put to use.
Yes, if they were kept together and put out to earn interest.
I would play Lord Pandarus of Phrygia, sir, to bring a / Cressida to this Troilus.
I'd like to play Lord Pandarus of Phrygia, sir, and bring a Cressida to this Troilus.
I understand you, sir; 'tis well begged.
I understand you, sir. That's cleverly begged.

The matter, I hope, is not great, sir, begging but a beggar: / Cressida was a beggar. My lady is within, sir. I will construe to / them whence you come; who you are and what you would are out of / my welkin: I might say element; but the word is overworn.

It's no great thing, I hope, sir, begging for a beggar: Cressida ended up a beggar. My lady is in, sir. I'll explain to them where you've come from. Who you are and what you want is outside my sky; I might say 'element', but that word is worn out.

This fellow's wise enough to play the fool; / And, to do that well, craves a kind of wit: / He must observe their mood on whom he jests, / The quality of persons, and the time; / And, like the haggard, check at every feather / That comes before his eye. This is a practice / As full of labour as a wise man's art: / For folly, that he wisely shows, is fit; / But wise men, folly-fallen, quite taint their wit.

This fellow is wise enough to play the fool, and to do that well needs a kind of intelligence. He has to watch the mood of the people he jokes about, their rank, and the right moment; and like a wild hawk, he has to swoop at every feather that comes in front of his eye. This is a skill as hard as a wise man's profession. The folly he shows so wisely is fitting; but wise men who fall into folly completely ruin their reputation for sense.
I hope, sir, you are; and I am yours.
I hope you are, sir; and I am yours.
Will you encounter the house? my niece is desirous you / should enter, if your trade be to her.
Will you approach the house? My niece wants you to come in, if your business is with her.
I am bound to your niece, sir: I mean, she is the list of my / voyage.
I am bound for your niece, sir; I mean, she is the destination of my voyage.
Taste your legs, sir; put them to motion.
Try your legs, sir; put them in motion.
My legs do better understand me, sir, than I understand what / you mean by bidding me taste my legs.
My legs understand me better, sir, than I understand what you mean by telling me to try my legs.
I mean, to go, sir, to enter.
I mean to go, sir, to enter.
I will answer you with gait and entrance: but we are prevented.
I'll answer you by going and entering. But we've been anticipated.
Most excellent accomplished lady, the heavens rain odours on you!
Most excellent, accomplished lady, may the heavens rain perfumes on you!
That youth's a rare courtier: 'Rain odours'! well.
That youth is a fine courtier. 'Rain perfumes'! Very good.
My matter hath no voice, lady, but to your own most pregnant / and vouchsafed ear.
My business can be spoken only to your own most receptive and gracious ear, lady.
'Perfumes', 'receptive' and 'gracious'. I'll learn all three of those ready for use.
Let the garden door be shut, and leave me to my hearing.
Let the garden door be shut, and leave me to hear him.
My duty, madam, and most humble service.
My duty, madam, and most humble service.
Cesario is your servant's name, fair princess.
Cesario is your servant's name, fair princess.
My servant, sir! 'Twas never merry world, / Since lowly feigning was call'd compliment: / You are servant to the Count Orsino, youth.
My servant, sir! The world has never been happy since false humility was called good manners. You are Count Orsino's servant, young man.
And he is yours, and his must needs be yours; / Your servant's servant is your servant, madam.
And he is yours, and what is his must be yours. Your servant's servant is your servant, madam.
For him, I think not on him: for his thoughts, / Would they were blanks rather than fill'd with me!
As for him, I don't think about him. As for his thoughts, I wish they were blank rather than filled with me!
Madam, I come to whet your gentle thoughts / On his behalf:—
Madam, I have come to sharpen your gentle thoughts on his behalf...
O, by your leave, I pray you: / I bade you never speak again of him: / But, would you undertake another suit, / I had rather hear you to solicit that / Than music from the spheres.
Oh, excuse me, please. I told you never to speak of him again. But if you would plead for someone else, I'd rather hear you ask for that than hear the music of the heavenly spheres.

Give me leave, beseech you: I did send, / After the last enchantment you did here, / A ring in chase of you; so did I abuse / Myself, my servant, and, I fear me, you: / Under your hard construction must I sit; / To force that on you, in a shameful cunning, / Which you knew none of yours. What might you think? / Have you not set mine honour at the stake, / And baited it with all the unmuzzl'd thoughts / That tyrannous heart can think? To one of your receiving / Enough is shown: a cypress, not a bosom, / Hides my heart: so let me hear you speak.

Let me speak, I beg you. After the last spell you cast here, I sent a ring after you. In doing so I wronged myself, my servant and, I'm afraid, you. I must sit under your harsh judgment for forcing on you, with shameful trickery, something you knew wasn't yours. What must you think? Haven't you tied my honour to the stake and set on it all the unmuzzled thoughts a cruel heart can think? To someone as quick as you, I've shown enough: a thin veil, not a bosom, hides my heart. So let me hear you speak.
No, not a grise; for 'tis a vulgar proof / That very oft we pity enemies.
No, not a single step, because it's common experience that we very often pity our enemies.

Why, then, methinks 'tis time to smile again: / O world, how apt the poor are to be proud! / If one should be a prey, how much the better / To fall before the lion than the wolf!  [Clock strikes.] / The clock upbraids me with the waste of time.— / Be not afraid, good youth, I will not have you: / And yet, when wit and youth is come to harvest, / Your wife is like to reap a proper man. / There lies your way, due-west.

Why, then, I think it's time to smile again. Oh world, how ready the poor are to be proud! If one has to be a victim, how much better to fall to the lion than to the wolf! [Clock strikes] The clock scolds me for wasting time. Don't be afraid, good youth, I won't have you. And yet, when your wit and youth have grown to harvest, your wife is likely to reap a fine man. There's your way, due west.
Then westward-ho: / Grace and good disposition 'tend your ladyship! / You'll nothing, madam, to my lord by me?
Then westward ho! May grace and good spirits be with your ladyship! You have no message, madam, for my lord through me?
Stay: / I pr'ythee tell me what thou think'st of me.
Wait. Please tell me what you think of me.
That you do think you are not what you are.
That you think you are not what you are.
If I think so, I think the same of you.
If I think so, I think the same of you.
Then think you right; I am not what I am.
Then you think right: I am not what I am.
I would you were as I would have you be!
I wish you were what I would like you to be!
Would it be better, madam, than I am, / I wish it might; for now I am your fool.
Would that be better, madam, than what I am? I hope it would, because now you're making a fool of me.

O what a deal of scorn looks beautiful / In the contempt and anger of his lip! / A murd'rous guilt shows not itself more soon / Than love that would seem hid: love's night is noon. / Cesario, by the roses of the spring, / By maidhood, honour, truth, and everything, / I love thee so that, maugre all thy pride, / Nor wit, nor reason, can my passion hide. / Do not extort thy reasons from this clause, / For, that I woo, thou therefore hast no cause: / But rather reason thus with reason fetter: / Love sought is good, but given unsought is better.

Oh, how beautiful scorn looks in the contempt and anger of his lip! A murderer's guilt doesn't show itself faster than a love that tries to hide; love's night is as clear as noon. Cesario, by the roses of the spring, by maidenhood, honour, truth and everything, I love you so much that, despite all your pride, neither wit nor reason can hide my passion. Don't argue from this that, because I'm the one wooing, you have no reason to woo me. Rather, tie that reasoning with this better reason: love that is sought is good, but love given unsought is better.

By innocence I swear, and by my youth, / I have one heart, one bosom, and one truth, / And that no woman has; nor never none / Shall mistress be of it, save I alone. / And so adieu, good madam; never more / Will I my master's tears to you deplore.

I swear by innocence and by my youth, I have one heart, one breast and one truth, and no woman has it, nor will any woman ever be mistress of it, except me alone. And so goodbye, good madam; I will never again come to you to lament my master's tears.
Yet come again: for thou, perhaps, mayst move / That heart, which now abhors, to like his love.
But come again, because perhaps you can move this heart, which hates his love now, to like it.
No, faith, I'll not stay a jot longer.
No, honestly, I won't stay a moment longer.
Thy reason, dear venom: give thy reason.
Your reason, my dear angry one; give your reason.
You must needs yield your reason, Sir Andrew.
You must give your reason, Sir Andrew.
Marry, I saw your niece do more favours to the count's / servingman than ever she bestowed upon me; I saw't i' the / orchard.
Well, I saw your niece show more favour to the Count's servant than she has ever shown me. I saw it in the orchard.
Did she see thee the while, old boy? tell me that.
Did she see you while she was doing it, old boy? Tell me that.
As plain as I see you now.
As plainly as I see you now.
This was a great argument of love in her toward you.
That was a great proof of her love for you.
'Slight! will you make an ass o' me?
By God's light! Are you making an ass of me?
I will prove it legitimate, sir, upon the oaths of judgment / and reason.
I'll prove it's sound, sir, on the testimony of judgment and reason.
And they have been grand jurymen since before Noah was a / sailor.
And they've been grand jurors since before Noah was a sailor.

She did show favour to the youth in your sight only to / exasperate you, to awake your dormouse valour, to put fire in / your heart and brimstone in your liver. You should then have / accosted her; and with some excellent jests, fire-new from the / mint, you should have banged the youth into dumbness. This was / looked for at your hand, and this was baulked: the double gilt of / this opportunity you let time wash off, and you are now sailed / into the north of my lady's opinion; where you will hang like an / icicle on Dutchman's beard, unless you do redeem it by some / laudable attempt either of valour or policy.

She showed favour to the youth in front of you only to provoke you, to wake up your sleepy courage, to put fire in your heart and brimstone in your liver. You should have approached her then, and with some excellent jokes, brand new from the mint, you should have knocked the youth speechless. That's what was expected of you, and you missed it. You let time wash the double gilding off this opportunity, and now you've sailed into the cold north of my lady's opinion, where you'll hang like an icicle on a Dutchman's beard unless you redeem yourself with some praiseworthy act of courage or cunning.
And't be any way, it must be with valour: for policy I / hate; I had as lief be a Brownist as a politician.
If it's to be either, it must be courage, because I hate cunning. I'd as soon be a religious separatist as a schemer.

Why, then, build me thy fortunes upon the basis of / valour. Challenge me the count's youth to fight with him; hurt / him in eleven places; my niece shall take note of it: and assure / thyself there is no love-broker in the world can more prevail in / man's commendation with woman than report of valour.

Why then, build your fortune on courage. Challenge the Count's youth to fight you. Wound him in eleven places; my niece will take note of it. And believe me, there's no matchmaker in the world who can recommend a man to a woman better than a reputation for bravery.
There is no way but this, Sir Andrew.
There's no other way, Sir Andrew.
Will either of you bear me a challenge to him?
Will either of you take a challenge to him for me?

Go, write it in a martial hand; be curst and brief; it is / no matter how witty, so it be eloquent and full of invention; / taunt him with the licence of ink; if thou 'thou'st' him some / thrice, it shall not be amiss; and as many lies as will lie in / thy sheet of paper, although the sheet were big enough for the / bed of Ware in England, set 'em down; go about it. Let there be / gall enough in thy ink; though thou write with a goose-pen, no / matter. About it.

Go and write it in a soldierly hand. Be fierce and brief. It doesn't matter how witty it is, as long as it's eloquent and full of invention. Insult him with all the freedom ink gives you. If you call him 'thou' three times or so, it won't do any harm. Put down as many lies as will fit on your sheet of paper, even if the sheet were big enough for the great bed of Ware in England. Get on with it. Let there be enough bitterness in your ink, though it doesn't matter if you write with a goose quill. Get on with it.
We'll call thee at the cubiculo. Go.
We'll call for you at your little room. Go.
This is a dear manakin to you, Sir Toby.
He's a dear little puppet to you, Sir Toby.
I have been dear to him, lad; some two thousand strong, or so.
I've been dear to him, lad: about two thousand ducats' worth, or so.
We shall have a rare letter from him: but you'll not deliver it.
We'll get a fine letter from him. But you won't deliver it?

Never trust me then; and by all means stir on the youth / to an answer. I think oxen and wainropes cannot hale them / together. For Andrew, if he were opened and you find so much / blood in his liver as will clog the foot of a flea, I'll eat the / rest of the anatomy.

Never trust me again if I don't. And by all means provoke the youth to reply. I don't think oxen and wagon ropes could drag them together. As for Andrew, if he were cut open and you found as much blood in his liver as would clog the foot of a flea, I'll eat the rest of his body.
And his opposite, the youth, bears in his visage no great / presage of cruelty.
And his opponent, the youth, doesn't show much sign of cruelty in his face.
Look where the youngest wren of nine comes.
Look, here comes the smallest wren of the brood.

If you desire the spleen, and will laugh yourselves into / stitches, follow me: yond gull Malvolio is turned heathen, a very / renegado; for there is no Christian, that means to be saved by / believing rightly, can ever believe such impossible passages of / grossness. He's in yellow stockings.

If you want a fit of laughter and to laugh yourselves into stitches, follow me. That fool Malvolio has turned heathen, a real traitor to the faith, because no Christian who hopes to be saved by believing correctly could ever believe such ridiculous nonsense. He's in yellow stockings.

Most villainously; like a pedant that keeps a school i' the / church.—I have dogged him like his murderer. He does obey every / point of the letter that I dropped to betray him. He does smile / his face into more lines than is in the new map, with the / augmentation of the Indies: you have not seen such a thing as / 'tis; I can hardly forbear hurling things at him. I know my lady / will strike him; if she do, he'll smile and take't for a great / favour.

Horribly, like a schoolmaster who teaches in the church. I've followed him like his murderer. He's obeying every detail of the letter I dropped to trap him. He smiles his face into more lines than there are on the new map with the Indies added. You've never seen anything like it. I can hardly stop myself throwing things at him. I know my lady will strike him; if she does, he'll smile and take it as a great favour.
Come, bring us, bring us where he is.
Come on, take us, take us to where he is.
I would not by my will have troubled you; / But since you make your pleasure of your pains, / I will no further chide you.
I wouldn't willingly have troubled you; but since you take pleasure in your trouble, I won't scold you any more.

I could not stay behind you: my desire, / More sharp than filed steel, did spur me forth; / And not all love to see you,—though so much, / As might have drawn one to a longer voyage,— / But jealousy what might befall your travel, / Being skilless in these parts; which to a stranger, / Unguided and unfriended, often prove / Rough and unhospitable. My willing love, / The rather by these arguments of fear, / Set forth in your pursuit.

I couldn't stay behind. My desire, sharper than filed steel, drove me on. It wasn't only love of seeing you, though that was strong enough to make a man take a longer voyage, but anxiety about what might happen to you on your travels, since you don't know these parts, which often prove rough and unwelcoming to a stranger without a guide or friends. My willing love, made keener by these fears, set out after you.

My kind Antonio, / I can no other answer make but thanks, / And thanks, and ever thanks. Often good turns / Are shuffled off with such uncurrent pay; / But were my worth, as is my conscience, firm, / You should find better dealing. What's to do? / Shall we go see the reliques of this town?

My kind Antonio, I can give no answer but thanks, and thanks, and always thanks. Good deeds are often brushed off with such worthless payment; but if my wealth were as solid as my sense of obligation, you would be better rewarded. What shall we do? Shall we go and see the sights of this town?
To-morrow, sir; best, first, go see your lodging.
Tomorrow, sir. It's best to go and find your lodgings first.
I am not weary, and 'tis long to night; / I pray you, let us satisfy our eyes / With the memorials and the things of fame / That do renown this city.
I'm not tired, and it's a long time till night. Please, let's feast our eyes on the monuments and famous things that make this city renowned.

Would you'd pardon me; / I do not without danger walk these streets: / Once in a sea-fight, 'gainst the count, his galleys, / I did some service; of such note, indeed, / That, were I ta'en here, it would scarce be answered.

Please excuse me. It's dangerous for me to walk these streets. I once fought in a sea battle against the Count's galleys, and did such notable damage that if I were captured here I'd hardly be able to defend myself.
Belike you slew great number of his people.
I suppose you killed a great number of his people.

The offence is not of such a bloody nature; / Albeit the quality of the time and quarrel / Might well have given us bloody argument. / It might have since been answered in repaying / What we took from them; which, for traffic's sake, / Most of our city did: only myself stood out; / For which, if I be lapsed in this place, / I shall pay dear.

The offence wasn't so bloody, although the circumstances of the time and the quarrel could well have given us cause for bloodshed. It could have been settled since by repaying what we took from them, which most of our city did for the sake of trade. Only I refused; and if I'm caught here, I'll pay dearly for it.
Do not then walk too open.
Then don't walk about too openly.

It doth not fit me. Hold, sir, here's my purse; / In the south suburbs, at the Elephant, / Is best to lodge: I will bespeak our diet / Whiles you beguile the time and feed your knowledge / With viewing of the town; there shall you have me.

It wouldn't suit me. Wait, sir, here's my purse. The best place to stay is at the Elephant, in the southern suburbs. I'll order our meals while you pass the time and improve your knowledge by seeing the town. You'll find me there.
Why should I have your purse?
Haply your eye shall light upon some toy / You have desire to purchase; and your store, / I think, is not for idle markets, sir.
Perhaps your eye will light on some trinket you'd like to buy, and I don't think your funds are meant for luxuries, sir.
I'll be your purse-bearer, and leave you for an hour.
I'll carry your purse and leave you for an hour.

I have sent after him. He says he'll come; / How shall I feast him? what bestow on him? / For youth is bought more oft than begged or borrowed. / I speak too loud.— / Where's Malvolio?—He is sad and civil, / And suits well for a servant with my fortunes;— / Where is Malvolio?

I've sent for him; he says he'll come. How shall I entertain him? What shall I give him? Youth is bought more often than it's begged or borrowed. I'm speaking too loudly. Where's Malvolio? He is serious and respectful, and suits a servant for someone in my situation. Where is Malvolio?
He's coming, madam: / But in very strange manner. He is sure possessed.
He's coming, madam, but in a very strange manner. He must be possessed.
Why, what's the matter? does he rave?
Why, what's the matter? Is he raving?
No, madam, he does nothing but smile: your ladyship were / best to have some guard about you if he come; / For, sure, the man is tainted in his wits.
No, madam, he does nothing but smile. Your ladyship had better have someone to protect you if he comes, because the man is certainly sick in his mind.
Go call him hither.—I'm as mad as he, / If sad and merry madness equal be.—
Go and call him here. I'm as mad as he is, if sad madness and merry madness are equal.
Smil'st thou? / I sent for thee upon a sad occasion.
Are you smiling? I sent for you on a serious matter.

Sad, lady? I could be sad: this does make some / obstruction in the blood, this cross-gartering. But what of that? / If it please the eye of one, it is with me as the very true / sonnet is: 'Please one and please all.'

Serious, lady? I could be serious. This cross-gartering does cause some blockage in the blood. But what does that matter? If it pleases the eye of one person, then it's with me as the very true poem says: 'Please one and please all.'
Why, how dost thou, man? what is the matter with thee?
Why, how are you, man? What's the matter with you?
Not black in my mind, though yellow in my legs. / It did come to his hands, and commands shall be executed. / I think we do know the sweet Roman hand.
Not black in my mind, though yellow in my legs. It did come into his hands, and commands shall be carried out. I think we know that sweet Italian handwriting.
Wilt thou go to bed, Malvolio?
Do you want to go to bed, Malvolio?
To bed? ay, sweetheart; and I'll come to thee.
To bed? Yes, sweetheart, and I'll come to you.
God comfort thee! Why dost thou smile so, and kiss thy hand so / oft?
God help you! Why do you smile like that and kiss your hand so often?
At your request? Yes; nightingales answer daws.
Answer you? Yes; nightingales answer jackdaws.
Why appear you with this ridiculous boldness before my lady?
Why do you appear before my lady with this ridiculous boldness?
'Be not afraid of greatness':—'twas well writ.
'Don't be afraid of greatness.' That was well written.
What meanest thou by that, Malvolio?
What do you mean by that, Malvolio?
'And some have greatness thrust upon them.'
'And some have greatness thrust upon them.'
'Go to: thou art made, if thou desirest to be so:'—
'Go on, your fortune is made, if you want it to be...'
'If not, let me see thee a servant still.'
'If not, let me see you a servant still.'
Why, this is very midsummer madness.
Why, this is pure midsummer madness.
Madam, the young gentleman of the Count Orsino's is / returned; I could hardly entreat him back; he attends your / ladyship's pleasure.
Madam, Count Orsino's young gentleman has come back. I could hardly persuade him to return. He's waiting for your ladyship.
Good Maria, let this fellow be looked to. Where's my cousin Toby? / Let some of my people have a special care of him; I would not / have him miscarry for the half of my dowry.
Good Maria, make sure this fellow is looked after. Where's my cousin Toby? Let some of my servants take special care of him; I wouldn't want him harmed for half my fortune.

O, ho! do you come near me now? No worse man than Sir / Toby to look to me? This concurs directly with the letter: she / sends him on purpose, that I may appear stubborn to him; for she / incites me to that in the letter. 'Cast thy humble slough,' says / she;—'be opposite with a kinsman, surly with servants,—let thy / tongue tang with arguments of state,—put thyself into the trick / of singularity;—and consequently, sets down the manner how; as, / a sad face, a reverend carriage, a slow tongue, in the habit of / some sir of note, and so forth. I have limed her; but it is / Jove's doing, and Jove make me thankful! And, when she went away / now, 'Let this fellow be looked to;' Fellow! not Malvolio, nor / after my degree, but fellow. Why, everything adheres together; / that no dram of a scruple, no scruple of a scruple, no obstacle, / no incredulous or unsafe circumstance,—What can be said? / Nothing, that can be, can come between me and the full prospect / of my hopes. Well, Jove, not I, is the doer of this, and he is to / be thanked.

Oh ho! Do you understand me now? No lesser man than Sir Toby to look after me? This agrees exactly with the letter. She's sending him on purpose so that I can be rude to him, because she urges me to that in the letter. 'Throw off your humble skin,' she says, 'be hostile to a relative, rude to servants; let your tongue ring out political arguments; adopt the habit of being different.' And then she sets down how to do it: a serious face, a dignified bearing, slow speech, in the manner of some important gentleman, and so on. I've caught her like a bird in lime; but it's Jove's doing, and may Jove make me thankful! And when she left just now, 'Let this fellow be looked after.' Fellow! Not Malvolio, not according to my rank, but fellow, meaning companion. Why, everything fits together, so that not a scrap of doubt, not a scrap of a scrap, no obstacle, no unlikely or uncertain circumstance... What can be said? Nothing that exists can come between me and the full view of my hopes. Well, Jove, not I, has done this, and he is to be thanked.
Which way is he, in the name of sanctity? If all the / devils of hell be drawn in little, and Legion himself possessed / him, yet I'll speak to him.
Where is he, in the name of all that's holy? Even if all the devils in hell were squeezed into him, and Legion himself possessed him, I'll still speak to him.
Here he is, here he is:—How is't with you, sir? how is't with / you, man?
Here he is, here he is. How are you, sir? How are you, man?
Go off; I discard you; let me enjoy my private; go off.
Go away. I dismiss you. Let me enjoy my privacy. Go away.
Lo, how hollow the fiend speaks within him! did not I tell / you?—Sir Toby, my lady prays you to have a care of him.
Listen, how hollow the devil sounds inside him! Didn't I tell you? Sir Toby, my lady asks you to look after him.
Go to, go to; peace, peace, we must deal gently with him; / let me alone. How do you, Malvolio? how is't with you? What, man! / defy the devil: consider, he's an enemy to mankind.
Come now, come now. Quiet, quiet, we must deal gently with him. Leave him to me. How are you, Malvolio? How is it with you? Come, man, defy the devil! Remember, he's the enemy of mankind.
Do you know what you say?
Do you know what you're saying?
La you, an you speak ill of the devil, how he takes it at / heart! Pray God he be not bewitched.
Look at that: if you speak ill of the devil, how he takes it to heart! Pray God he isn't bewitched.
Carry his water to the wise woman.
Take a sample of his urine to the wise woman.
Marry, and it shall be done to-morrow morning, if I live. My / lady would not lose him for more than I'll say.
Indeed, it will be done tomorrow morning, if I live. My lady wouldn't lose him for more than I can say.
Pr'ythee hold thy peace; this is not the way. Do you not / see you move him? let me alone with him.
Please be quiet; this isn't the way. Don't you see you're upsetting him? Leave him to me.
No way but gentleness; gently, gently: the fiend is rough, / and will not be roughly used.
Only gentleness will work. Gently, gently. The devil is rough and won't be treated roughly.
Why, how now, my bawcock? how dost thou, chuck.
Why, how are you, my fine fellow? How are you, chick?
Ay, Biddy, come with me. What, man! 'tis not for gravity / to play at cherry-pit with Satan. Hang him, foul collier!
Yes, chicken, come with me. Come, man! It's not right for a serious man like you to play children's games with Satan. Hang him, the filthy coal-man!
Get him to say his prayers; good Sir Toby, get him to pray.
Get him to say his prayers. Good Sir Toby, get him to pray.
No, I warrant you, he will not hear of godliness.
No, I promise you, he won't listen to anything godly.
Go, hang yourselves all! you are idle shallow things: I / am not of your element; you shall know more hereafter.
Go and hang yourselves, all of you! You are idle, shallow things. I am not of your kind. You will hear more later.
If this were played upon a stage now, I could condemn it as / an improbable fiction.
If this were acted on a stage now, I would condemn it as an unbelievable story.
His very genius hath taken the infection of the device, man.
His very soul has caught the infection of our trick, man.
Nay, pursue him now; lest the device take air and taint.
No, go after him now, in case the trick is exposed to the air and goes bad.
Why, we shall make him mad indeed.
Why, we'll really make him mad.
The house will be the quieter.

Come, we'll have him in a dark room and bound. My niece / is already in the belief that he's mad; we may carry it thus, for / our pleasure and his penance, till our very pastime, tired out of / breath, prompt us to have mercy on him: at which time we will / bring the device to the bar, and crown thee for a finder of / madmen. But see, but see.

Come on, we'll put him in a dark room and tie him up. My niece already believes he's mad. We can keep it going like this, for our fun and his punishment, until our sport itself, worn out of breath, makes us take pity on him. Then we'll bring our plot before the court and crown you as a discoverer of madmen. But look, look.
More matter for a May morning.
Here's the challenge, read it; I warrant there's vinegar and / pepper in't.
Here's the challenge. Read it. I promise you there's vinegar and pepper in it.
Ay, is't, I warrant him; do but read.
Yes, it is, I promise. Just read it.
Give me. [Reads.] 'Youth, whatsoever thou art, thou art but a / scurvy fellow.'
Give it to me. [Reads] 'Youth, whatever you are, you are only a scurvy fellow.'
'Wonder not, nor admire not in thy mind, why I do / call thee so, for I will show thee no reason for't.'
[Reads] 'Don't wonder or be amazed in your mind why I call you that, because I won't give you any reason for it.'
A good note: that keeps you from the blow of the law.
A good point; that keeps you safe from the law.
'Thou comest to the Lady Olivia, and in my sight / she uses thee kindly: but thou liest in thy throat; that is not / the matter I challenge thee for.'
[Reads] 'You come to Lady Olivia, and in front of me she treats you kindly. But you lie in your throat; that isn't what I'm challenging you for.'
Very brief, and to exceeding good senseless.
Very brief, and exceedingly good... nonsense.
'I will waylay thee going home; where if it be / thy chance to kill me,'—
[Reads] 'I will ambush you on your way home, where, if you happen to kill me...'
'Thou kill'st me like a rogue and a villain.'
[Reads] '...you kill me like a rogue and a villain.'
Still you keep o' the windy side of the law. Good.
You still keep on the safe side of the law. Good.

'Fare thee well; and God have mercy upon one of / our souls! He may have mercy upon mine; but my hope is better, / and so look to thyself. Thy friend, as thou usest him, and thy / sworn enemy, Andrew Ague-Cheek.' / If this letter move him not, his legs cannot: I'll give't him.

[Reads] 'Farewell, and God have mercy on one of our souls! He may have mercy on mine, but I have better hopes, so look out for yourself. Your friend, depending on how you treat him, and your sworn enemy, Andrew Aguecheek.' If this letter doesn't move him, his legs can't. I'll give it to him.
You may have very fit occasion for't; he is now in some / commerce with my lady, and will by and by depart.
You may have a very good opportunity for it. He's talking with my lady now and will leave soon.

Go, Sir Andrew; scout me for him at the corner of the / orchard, like a bum-bailiff; so soon as ever thou seest him, / draw; and as thou drawest, swear horrible; for it comes to pass / oft that a terrible oath, with a swaggering accent sharply / twanged off, gives manhood more approbation than ever proof / itself would have earned him. Away.

Go, Sir Andrew. Lie in wait for him at the corner of the orchard, like a bailiff. As soon as you see him, draw your sword, and as you draw, swear horribly, because it often happens that a terrible oath, delivered sharply in a swaggering voice, wins a man more of a reputation for courage than actually proving it would ever have earned him. Off you go.
Nay, let me alone for swearing.
No, leave the swearing to me.

Now will not I deliver his letter; for the behaviour of / the young gentleman gives him out to be of good capacity and / breeding; his employment between his lord and my niece confirms / no less; therefore this letter, being so excellently ignorant, / will breed no terror in the youth: he will find it comes from a / clodpole. But, sir, I will deliver his challenge by word of / mouth, set upon Ague-cheek notable report of valour, and drive / the gentleman,—as I know his youth will aptly receive it,—into / a most hideous opinion of his rage, skill, fury, and impetuosity. / This will so fright them both that they will kill one another by / the look, like cockatrices.

Now I won't deliver his letter, because the young gentleman's behaviour shows he is intelligent and well brought up; his role as go-between for his lord and my niece confirms that. So this letter, being so splendidly ignorant, won't frighten the youth at all; he'll realise it comes from a blockhead. Instead, sir, I'll deliver his challenge in person, give Aguecheek a great reputation for courage, and drive the gentleman, since I know his youth will easily believe it, into a terrifying opinion of his rage, skill, fury and violence. This will frighten them both so much that they'll kill each other with a look, like basilisks.
Here he comes with your niece; give them way till he take / leave, and presently after him.
Here he comes with your niece. Keep out of their way until he says goodbye, and then go straight after him.
I will meditate the while upon some horrid message for a / challenge.
Meanwhile I'll think up some horrible message for a challenge.

I have said too much unto a heart of stone, / And laid mine honour too unchary on it: / There's something in me that reproves my fault; / But such a headstrong potent fault it is / That it but mocks reproof.

I have said too much to a heart of stone and risked my honour too carelessly on it. There's something in me that blames me for my fault, but it is such a stubborn, powerful fault that it just laughs at blame.
With the same 'haviour that your passion bears / Goes on my master's griefs.
My master's griefs carry on in exactly the same way as your passion.

Here, wear this jewel for me; 'tis my picture; / Refuse it not; it hath no tongue to vex you: / And, I beseech you, come again to-morrow. / What shall you ask of me that I'll deny, / That, honour saved, may upon asking give?

Here, wear this jewel for me; it's my portrait. Don't refuse it; it has no tongue to annoy you. And I beg you, come again tomorrow. What could you ask of me that I would refuse, if I could grant it without losing my honour?
Nothing but this, your true love for my master.
Only this: your true love for my master.
How with mine honour may I give him that / Which I have given to you?
How can I honourably give him what I have given to you?
I will release you from that.
Well, come again to-morrow. Fare thee well; / A fiend like thee might bear my soul to hell.
Well, come again tomorrow. Goodbye. A devil like you could carry my soul to hell.

That defence thou hast, betake thee to't. Of what nature / the wrongs are thou hast done him, I know not; but thy / intercepter, full of despite, bloody as the hunter, attends / thee at the orchard end: dismount thy tuck, be yare in thy / preparation, for thy assailant is quick, skilful, and deadly.

Whatever means of defence you have, get ready to use it. I don't know what wrongs you have done him, but the man waiting to ambush you, full of spite and as bloodthirsty as a hunter, is waiting for you at the end of the orchard. Draw your rapier and be quick in getting ready, because your attacker is quick, skilful and deadly.
You mistake, sir; I am sure no man hath any quarrel to me; / my remembrance is very free and clear from any image of offence / done to any man.
You're mistaken, sir. I'm sure no man has any quarrel with me. My memory is completely free and clear of any offence I've done to anyone.

You'll find it otherwise, I assure you: therefore, if you / hold your life at any price, betake you to your guard; for your / opposite hath in him what youth, strength, skill, and wrath, can / furnish man withal.
You'll find otherwise, I assure you. So if you value your life at all, get on your guard, because your opponent has everything that youth, strength, skill and rage can give a man.
I pray you, sir, what is he?

He is knight, dubbed with unhacked rapier and on carpet / consideration; but he is a devil in private brawl; souls and / bodies hath he divorced three; and his incensement at this moment / is so implacable that satisfaction can be none but by pangs of / death and sepulchre: hob, nob is his word; give't or take't.

He's a knight, dubbed with an unused sword for services at court, not in battle; but he's a devil in a private fight. He has separated three souls from their bodies, and his anger at this moment is so fierce that nothing will satisfy it but the pangs of death and the grave. 'Hit or miss' is his motto: give it or take it.

I will return again into the house and desire some conduct / of the lady. I am no fighter. I have heard of some kind of men / that put quarrels purposely on others to taste their valour: / belike this is a man of that quirk.
I'll go back into the house and ask the lady for an escort. I'm no fighter. I've heard of men who deliberately pick quarrels with others to test their courage; this must be a man with that quirk.

Sir, no; his indignation derives itself out of a very / competent injury; therefore, get you on and give him his desire. / Back you shall not to the house, unless you undertake that with / me which with as much safety you might answer him: therefore on, / or strip your sword stark naked; for meddle you must, that's / certain, or forswear to wear iron about you.

No, sir. His anger comes from a very real injury, so go on and give him what he wants. You won't go back to the house unless you take on with me what you could just as safely take on with him. So go on, or strip your sword naked, because fight you must, that's certain, or else give up wearing a sword at all.
This is as uncivil as strange. I beseech you, do me this / courteous office as to know of the knight what my offence to him / is; it is something of my negligence, nothing of my purpose.
This is as rude as it is strange. I beg you, do me the courtesy of finding out from the knight what my offence against him is. It must be something I did carelessly, nothing I did on purpose.
I will do so. Signior Fabian, stay you by this gentleman / till my return.
I will. Signor Fabian, stay with this gentleman until I come back.
Pray you, sir, do you know of this matter?
Please, sir, do you know anything about this?
I know the knight is incensed against you, even to a mortal / arbitrement; but nothing of the circumstance more.
I know the knight is furious with you, even to the point of fighting to the death, but I know nothing more about the circumstances.
I beseech you, what manner of man is he?
I beg you, what kind of man is he?

Nothing of that wonderful promise, to read him by his form, / as you are like to find him in the proof of his valour. He is / indeed, sir, the most skilful, bloody, and fatal opposite that / you could possibly have found in any part of Illyria. Will you / walk towards him? I will make your peace with him if I can.

Judging by his appearance, he doesn't look as remarkable as you're likely to find him when he proves his courage. He is indeed, sir, the most skilful, bloodthirsty and deadly opponent you could possibly have found anywhere in Illyria. Will you walk towards him? I'll make peace for you if I can.
I shall be much bound to you for't. I am one that would / rather go with sir priest than sir knight: I care not who knows / so much of my mettle.
I'll be very grateful to you for it. I'm someone who would rather keep company with a priest than a knight. I don't care who knows that much about my character.

Why, man, he's a very devil; I have not seen such a / virago. I had a pass with him, rapier, scabbard, and all, and he / gives me the stuck-in with such a mortal motion that it is / inevitable; and on the answer, he pays you as surely as your feet / hit the ground they step on. They say he has been fencer to the / Sophy.

Why, man, he's a real devil. I've never seen such a fierce fighter. I had a practice bout with him, rapier, scabbard and all, and he lunged at me with such a deadly movement that it was impossible to avoid. And when he parries, he hits you back as surely as your feet hit the ground they walk on. They say he was the Shah of Persia's fencing master.
Pox on't, I'll not meddle with him.
Damn it, I'll have nothing to do with him.
Ay, but he will not now be pacified: Fabian can scarce / hold him yonder.
Yes, but he won't be calmed down now. Fabian can hardly hold him back over there.

Plague on't; an I thought he had been valiant, and so / cunning in fence, I'd have seen him damned ere I'd have / challenged him. Let him let the matter slip and I'll give him / my horse, grey Capilet.
Plague on it! If I'd thought he was brave and so skilled at fencing, I'd have seen him damned before I challenged him. If he'll let the matter drop, I'll give him my horse, grey Capilet.
I'll make the motion. Stand here, make a good show on't; / this shall end without the perdition of souls. [Aside.] Marry, / I'll ride your horse as well as I ride you.
I'll make the offer. Stand here and put on a good show. This will end without anyone losing their soul. [Aside] Indeed, I'll ride your horse as well as I ride you.
I have his horse [To Fabian.] to take up the quarrel; I have / persuaded him the youth's a devil.
[To Fabian] I've got his horse to settle the quarrel. I've persuaded him the youth's a devil.
He is as horribly conceited of him; and pants and looks pale, as / if a bear were at his heels.
The youth has just as horrible an idea of him, and pants and looks pale, as if a bear were at his heels.

There's no remedy, sir: he will fight with you for's oath sake: / marry, he hath better bethought him of his quarrel, and he finds / that now scarce to be worth talking of: therefore, draw for the / supportance of his vow; he protests he will not hurt you.

There's no help for it, sir. He'll fight with you because of his oath. Though he's thought better of his quarrel and finds now that it's hardly worth talking about. So draw, to let him keep his vow; he swears he won't hurt you.
[Aside] Pray God defend me! A little thing would make me / tell them how much I lack of a man.
[Aside] God protect me! It wouldn't take much to make me tell them how far I am from being a man.
Give ground if you see him furious.
Back away if you see him getting furious.

Come, Sir Andrew, there's no remedy; the gentleman will, / for his honour's sake, have one bout with you: he cannot by the / duello avoid it; but he has promised me, as he is a gentleman and / a soldier, he will not hurt you. Come on: to't.

Come on, Sir Andrew, there's no help for it. The gentleman will have one bout with you for the sake of his honour; by the rules of duelling he can't avoid it. But he has promised me, as he's a gentleman and a soldier, that he won't hurt you. Come on, to it.
Pray God he keep his oath! / [Draws.]
Pray God he keeps his promise! [He draws]
I do assure you 'tis against my will. / [Draws.]
I assure you it's against my will. [She draws]
Put up your sword:—if this young gentleman / Have done offence, I take the fault on me; / If you offend him, I for him defy you. / [Drawing.]
Put away your sword. If this young gentleman has done anything wrong, I take the blame on myself. If you are the one wronging him, I challenge you on his behalf. [He draws]
You, sir! why, what are you?
You, sir! Why, who are you?
One, sir, that for his love dares yet do more / Than you have heard him brag to you he will.
Someone, sir, who for love of him dares to do even more than you've heard him boast to you that he will.
Nay, if you be an undertaker, I am for you. / [Draws.]
Well, if you're going to take on other people's fights, I'm ready for you. [He draws]
O good Sir Toby, hold; here come the officers.
Oh good Sir Toby, stop! Here come the officers.
[To Antonio] I'll be with you anon.
[To Antonio] I'll deal with you later.
[To Sir Andrew.] Pray, sir, put your sword up, if you please.
[To Sir Andrew] Please, sir, put your sword away, if you don't mind.
Marry, will I, sir; and for that I promised you, I'll be / as good as my word. He will bear you easily and reins well.
Indeed I will, sir. And as for what I promised you, I'll be as good as my word. He's an easy ride and responds well to the reins.
This is the man; do thy office.
This is the man. Do your duty.
Antonio, I arrest thee at the suit / Of Count Orsino.
Antonio, I arrest you on the orders of Count Orsino.
You've mistaken me for someone else, sir.
No, sir, no jot; I know your favour well, / Though now you have no sea-cap on your head.— / Take him away; he knows I know him well.
No, sir, not at all. I know your face well, though you don't have a sailor's cap on your head now. Take him away; he knows I know him well.

I must obey.—This comes with seeking you; / But there's no remedy; I shall answer it. / What will you do? Now my necessity / Makes me to ask you for my purse. It grieves me / Much more for what I cannot do for you / Than what befalls myself. You stand amazed; / But be of comfort.

I must obey. [To Viola] This comes of looking for you; but there's no help for it. I'll have to answer for it. What will you do? Now my need forces me to ask you for my purse. I'm much more upset about what I can't do for you than about what happens to me. You look amazed, but cheer up.
I must entreat of you some of that money.
I must ask you for some of that money.

What money, sir? / For the fair kindness you have showed me here, / And part being prompted by your present trouble, / Out of my lean and low ability / I'll lend you something; my having is not much; / I'll make division of my present with you: / Hold, there is half my coffer.

What money, sir? Because of the kindness you've shown me here, and partly moved by your present trouble, I'll lend you something from my small and meagre means. I don't have much; I'll share what I have with you. Here, that's half my money.

Will you deny me now? / Is't possible that my deserts to you / Can lack persuasion? Do not tempt my misery, / Lest that it make me so unsound a man / As to upbraid you with those kindnesses / That I have done for you.

Are you going to deny me now? Is it possible that what I've done for you can fail to persuade you? Don't push my misery too far, in case it makes me so ungentlemanly that I reproach you with the kindnesses I've done for you.

I know of none, / Nor know I you by voice or any feature: / I hate ingratitude more in a man / Than lying, vainness, babbling, drunkenness, / Or any taint of vice whose strong corruption / Inhabits our frail blood.

I don't know of any, and I don't know you by your voice or by any of your features. I hate ingratitude in a man more than lying, vanity, chattering, drunkenness, or any trace of vice whose strong corruption lives in our weak flesh.
Come, sir, I pray you go.

Let me speak a little. This youth that you see here / I snatched one half out of the jaws of death, / Relieved him with such sanctity of love,— / And to his image, which methought did promise / Most venerable worth, did I devotion.

Let me speak a little. This youth you see here I snatched half dead from the jaws of death, cared for him with such holy love, and worshipped his image, which I thought promised the most honourable worth.
What's that to us? The time goes by; away.
What's that to us? Time is passing. Away!

But O how vile an idol proves this god! / Thou hast, Sebastian, done good feature shame. / In nature there's no blemish but the mind; / None can be call'd deform'd but the unkind: / Virtue is beauty; but the beauteous-evil / Are empty trunks, o'erflourished by the devil.

But oh, how vile an idol this god turns out to be! Sebastian, you have shamed your good looks. In nature there's no flaw except in the mind; no one can be called deformed except the unkind. Virtue is beauty; but people who are beautiful and evil are empty chests, decorated all over by the devil.
The man grows mad; away with him. Come, come, sir.
The man's going mad. Away with him! Come on, come on, sir.
Methinks his words do from such passion fly / That he believes himself; so do not I. / Prove true, imagination; O prove true, / That I, dear brother, be now ta'en for you!
His words come from such strong feeling that he believes them himself. I don't, yet. Imagination, prove true; oh, prove true, that I, dear brother, have just been mistaken for you!
Come hither, knight; come hither, Fabian; we'll whisper / o'er a couplet or two of most sage saws.
Come here, knight; come here, Fabian. We'll whisper a wise saying or two.

He named Sebastian; I my brother know / Yet living in my glass; even such and so / In favour was my brother; and he went / Still in this fashion, colour, ornament, / For him I imitate. O, if it prove, / Tempests are kind, and salt waves fresh in love!

He named Sebastian. I know my brother is still alive in my mirror. My brother looked exactly like this, and he always went dressed in this style, colour and decoration, because it's him I'm imitating. Oh, if it proves true, storms are kind, and salt waves are fresh with love!
A very dishonest paltry boy, and more a coward than a / hare: his dishonesty appears in leaving his friend here in / necessity, and denying him; and for his cowardship, ask Fabian.
A very dishonourable, worthless boy, and more of a coward than a hare. His dishonour shows in leaving his friend here in need and disowning him; and as for his cowardice, ask Fabian.
A coward, a most devout coward, religious in it.
A coward, a most devoted coward, religious about it.
'Slid, I'll after him again and beat him.
By God's eyelid, I'll go after him again and beat him.
Do, cuff him soundly, but never draw thy sword.
Do. Thump him soundly, but never draw your sword.
Come on, let's see what happens.
I dare lay any money 'twill be nothing yet.
I'll bet any money it will come to nothing yet.
Will you make me believe that I am not sent for you?
Are you trying to make me believe I wasn't sent for you?
Go to, go to, thou art a foolish fellow; / Let me be clear of thee.
Come on, come on, you're a foolish fellow. Leave me alone.

Well held out, i' faith! No, I do not know you; nor I am not / sent to you by my lady, to bid you come speak with her; nor your / name is not Master Cesario; nor this is not my nose neither.— / Nothing that is so is so.

Well kept up, honestly! No, I don't know you; and I haven't been sent to you by my lady to ask you to come and speak with her; and your name isn't Master Cesario; and this isn't my nose either. Nothing that is so is so.
I pr'ythee vent thy folly somewhere else. Thou know'st not me.
Please go and vent your foolery somewhere else. You don't know me.

Vent my folly! he has heard that word of some great man, and / now applies it to a fool. Vent my folly! I am afraid this great / lubber, the world, will prove a cockney.—I pr'ythee now, ungird / thy strangeness, and tell me what I shall vent to my lady. Shall / I vent to her that thou art coming?

Vent my folly! He's heard that word from some great man and now he applies it to a fool. Vent my folly! I'm afraid this great lump, the world, will turn out to be a sissy. Please now, drop your strange act and tell me what I shall vent to my lady. Shall I vent to her that you're coming?
I pr'ythee, foolish Greek, depart from me; / There's money for thee; if you tarry longer / I shall give worse payment.
Please, you silly joker, go away. There's money for you. If you stay any longer I'll pay you worse.
By my troth, thou hast an open hand:—These wise men that / give fools money get themselves a good report after fourteen / years' purchase.
Honestly, you've got a generous hand. These wise men who give fools money earn themselves a good reputation, though it costs them fourteen years' rent.
Now, sir, have I met you again? there's for you. / [Striking Sebastian.]
Now, sir, have I met you again? Take that! [He strikes Sebastian]
Why, there's for thee, and there, and there. / Are all the people mad?
Why, take that, and that, and that! Is everyone mad?
Hold, sir, or I'll throw your dagger o'er the house.
Stop, sir, or I'll throw your dagger over the house.
This will I tell my lady straight. I would not be in some of / your coats for twopence.
I'll tell my lady about this straight away. I wouldn't be in some of your shoes for twopence.
Nay, let him alone; I'll go another way to work with / him; I'll have an action of battery against him, if there be any / law in Illyria: though I struck him first, yet it's no matter for / that.
No, leave him alone. I'll find another way to deal with him. I'll sue him for assault, if there's any law in Illyria. Though I hit him first, that doesn't matter.
Come, sir, I will not let you go. Come, my young soldier, / put up your iron: you are well fleshed; come on.
Come on, sir, I won't let you go. Come, my young soldier, put away your sword. You've had a taste of blood; come on.
I will be free from thee. What wouldst thou now? / If thou dar'st tempt me further, draw thy sword. / [Draws.]
I'll be free of you. What do you want now? If you dare to provoke me further, draw your sword. [He draws]
What, what? Nay, then I must have an ounce or two of this / malapert blood from you. / [Draws.]
What, what? Well then, I must have an ounce or two of your cheeky blood. [He draws]
Hold, Toby; on thy life, I charge thee hold.
Stop, Toby! On your life, I order you to stop.

Will it be ever thus? Ungracious wretch, / Fit for the mountains and the barbarous caves, / Where manners ne'er were preach'd! Out of my sight! / Be not offended, dear Cesario!— / Rudesby, be gone!—I pr'ythee, gentle friend,

Will it always be like this? Graceless wretch, fit for the mountains and the savage caves, where good manners were never taught! Get out of my sight! Don't be offended, dear Cesario. Ruffian, be gone! Please, gentle friend,

Let thy fair wisdom, not thy passion, sway / In this uncivil and unjust extent / Against thy peace. Go with me to my house, / And hear thou there how many fruitless pranks / This ruffian hath botch'd up, that thou thereby / Mayst smile at this: thou shalt not choose but go; / Do not deny. Beshrew his soul for me, / He started one poor heart of mine in thee.

let your good sense, not your anger, rule you in this rude and unjust attack on your peace. Come with me to my house, and hear there how many pointless pranks this ruffian has cobbled together, so that you can smile at this one. You must come; don't refuse. Curse his soul for me; he frightened my poor heart, which lives in you.
What relish is in this? how runs the stream? / Or I am mad, or else this is a dream:— / Let fancy still my sense in Lethe steep; / If it be thus to dream, still let me sleep!

What does this mean? Which way is the current flowing? Either I'm mad, or else this is a dream. Let my imagination keep my senses drowned in forgetfulness; if this is what it is to dream, let me sleep on!
Nay, come, I pr'ythee. Would thou'dst be ruled by me!
Come, please. I wish you'd let me guide you!
O, say so, and so be!
Oh, say so, and let it be so!
Nay, I pr'ythee, put on this gown and this beard; make him / believe thou art Sir Topas the curate; do it quickly: I'll call / Sir Toby the whilst.
Now please, put on this gown and this beard. Make him believe you're Sir Topas the curate. Be quick. I'll call Sir Toby meanwhile.

Well, I'll put it on, and I will dissemble myself in't; and / I would I were the first that ever dissembled in such a gown. I / am not tall enough to become the function well: nor lean enough / to be thought a good student: but to be said, an honest man and a / good housekeeper, goes as fairly as to say, a careful man and a / great scholar. The competitors enter.

Well, I'll put it on and disguise myself in it; and I wish I were the first man who ever told lies in a gown like this. I'm not tall enough to fill the role well, nor thin enough to be thought a good scholar. But to be called an honest man and a good host is as fine as being called a careful man and a great scholar. Here come my partners.

Bonos dies, Sir Toby: for as the old hermit of Prague, that / never saw pen and ink, very wittily said to a niece of King / Gorboduc, 'That that is, is'; so I, being master parson, am / master parson: for what is that but that? and is but is?

Good day, Sir Toby. For as the old hermit of Prague, who never saw pen and ink, very wittily said to a niece of King Gorboduc, 'That which is, is.' So I, being Master Parson, am Master Parson; for what is 'that' but 'that', and 'is' but 'is'?
What, hoa, I say,—Peace in this prison!
Hello there, I say! Peace be in this prison!
The knave counterfeits well; a good knave.
The rascal is a good actor; a good rascal.
[In an inner chamber.] Who calls there?
[From a dark inner room] Who's calling there?
Sir Topas the curate, who comes to visit Malvolio the / lunatic.
Sir Topas the curate, who has come to visit Malvolio the lunatic.
Sir Topas, Sir Topas, good Sir Topas, go to my lady.
Sir Topas, Sir Topas, good Sir Topas, go to my lady.
Out, hyperbolical fiend! how vexest thou this man? talkest thou / nothing but of ladies?
Out, you raving devil! How you torment this man! Do you talk about nothing but ladies?
Sir Topas, never was man thus wronged: good Sir Topas, do / not think I am mad; they have laid me here in hideous darkness.
Sir Topas, no man was ever wronged like this. Good Sir Topas, don't think I'm mad. They've shut me up here in terrible darkness.
Fie, thou dishonest Sathan! I call thee by the most modest / terms; for I am one of those gentle ones that will use the devil / himself with courtesy. Say'st thou that house is dark?
Shame on you, you lying Satan! I call you by the politest name I can, because I'm one of those gentle people who treat even the devil with courtesy. Do you say that room is dark?
As dark as hell, Sir Topas.
Why, it hath bay windows transparent as barricadoes, and the / clear storeys toward the south-north are as lustrous as ebony; / and yet complainest thou of obstruction?
Why, it has bay windows as transparent as barricades, and the high windows facing south-north are as bright as ebony; and yet you complain it's blocked?
I am not mad, Sir Topas; I say to you this house is dark.
I'm not mad, Sir Topas. I tell you, this room is dark.
Madman, thou errest. I say there is no darkness but / ignorance; in which thou art more puzzled than the Egyptians in / their fog.
Madman, you are wrong. I say there is no darkness but ignorance, and you're more lost in that than the Egyptians in their fog.

I say this house is as dark as ignorance, though / ignorance were as dark as hell; and I say there was never man / thus abused. I am no more mad than you are; make the trial of it / in any constant question.
I say this room is as dark as ignorance, even if ignorance were as dark as hell; and I say no man was ever so badly treated. I'm no more mad than you are. Test me with any reasonable question.
What is the opinion of Pythagoras concerning wild-fowl?
What is the opinion of Pythagoras about wild birds?
That the soul of our grandam might haply inhabit a bird.
That the soul of our grandmother might perhaps live in a bird.
What thinkest thou of his opinion?
What do you think of his opinion?
I think nobly of the soul, and no way approve his opinion.
I think nobly of the soul, and don't agree with his opinion at all.

Fare thee well. Remain thou still in darkness: thou shalt / hold the opinion of Pythagoras ere I will allow of thy wits; and / fear to kill a woodcock, lest thou dispossess the soul of thy / grandam. Fare thee well.
Goodbye. Stay in the dark. You'll have to accept the opinion of Pythagoras before I'll declare you sane, and be afraid to kill a woodcock in case you evict your grandmother's soul. Goodbye.
Nay, I am for all waters.
Oh, I can turn my hand to anything.
Thou mightst have done this without thy beard and gown: he / sees thee not.
You could have done this without your beard and gown. He can't see you.

To him in thine own voice, and bring me word how thou / findest him; I would we were well rid of this knavery. If he may / be conveniently delivered, I would he were; for I am now so far / in offence with my niece that I cannot pursue with any safety / this sport to the upshot. Come by and by to my chamber.

Go to him in your own voice and let me know how you find him. I wish we were well out of this trick. If he can be released without trouble, I wish he would be, because I'm now so far out of favour with my niece that I can't safely carry this game through to the end. Come to my room shortly.
[Singing.] 'Hey, Robin, jolly Robin, / Tell me how thy lady does.'
[Singing] 'Hey, Robin, jolly Robin, tell me how your lady is.'
