Good fool, as ever thou wilt deserve well at my hand, / help me to a candle, and pen, ink, and paper; as I am a / gentleman, I will live to be thankful to thee for't.
Good fool, if you ever want to be rewarded by me, help me to a candle, and pen, ink and paper. As I'm a gentleman, I'll live to be grateful to you for it.
Alas, sir, how fell you besides your five wits?
Oh dear, sir, how did you come to lose your five wits?
Fool, there was never man so notoriously abused; I am as well in / my wits, fool, as thou art.
Fool, no man was ever so outrageously wronged. I'm as sane as you are, fool.
But as well? then you are mad indeed, if you be no better in / your wits than a fool.
Only as sane? Then you're truly mad, if your wits are no better than a fool's.
They have here propertied me; keep me in darkness, send / ministers to me, asses, and do all they can to face me out of my / wits.
They've treated me like a piece of furniture here, keep me in the dark, send ministers to me, the asses, and do everything they can to bully me out of my wits.
Advise you what you say: the minister is here.—Malvolio, thy / wits the heavens restore! endeavour thyself to sleep, and leave / thy vain bibble-babble.
Be careful what you say; the minister is here. [In Sir Topas's voice] Malvolio, Malvolio, may the heavens restore your wits! Try to sleep, and stop your empty babbling.
Maintain no words with him, good fellow. Who, I, sir? not / I, sir. God b' wi' you, good Sir Topas.—Marry, amen.—I will / sir, I will.
[As Sir Topas] Have no conversation with him, good fellow. [As himself] Who, me, sir? Never, sir. Goodbye, good Sir Topas. [As Sir Topas] Indeed, amen. [As himself] I will, sir, I will.
Alas, sir, be patient. What say you, sir? I am shent for / speaking to you.
Oh dear, sir, be patient. What do you say, sir? I've been scolded for talking to you.
Good fool, help me to some light and some paper; / I tell thee I am as well in my wits as any man in Illyria.
Kind fool, fetch me a light and some paper. My mind is as sound as any man's in Illyria, I promise you.
Alas, I wish you were, sir!
By this hand, I am: Good fool, some ink, paper, and / light, and convey what I will set down to my lady; it shall / advantage thee more than ever the bearing of letter did.
By this hand, I am. Good fool, some ink, paper and light, and take what I write down to my lady. It will profit you more than carrying any letter ever did.
I will help you to't. But tell me true, are you not mad / indeed? or do you but counterfeit?
I'll help you get them. But tell me truly, aren't you really mad? Or are you just pretending?
Believe me, I am not; I tell thee true.
Believe me, I'm not. I'm telling you the truth.
Nay, I'll ne'er believe a madman till I see his brains. / I will fetch you light, and paper, and ink.
No, I'll never believe a madman till I see his brains. I'll fetch you light and paper and ink.
Fool, I'll requite it in the highest degree: I pr'ythee be / gone.
Fool, I'll reward you as highly as possible. Please go.

[Singing.] / 'I am gone, sir, / And anon, sir, / I'll be with you again, / In a trice, / Like to the old vice, / Your need to sustain; / Who with dagger of lath, / In his rage and his wrath, / Cries ah, ha! to the devil: / Like a mad lad, / Pare thy nails, dad. / Adieu, goodman drivel.

[Singing] 'I'm gone, sir, and soon, sir, I'll be with you again in a moment, like the old Vice in the plays, to help you in your need.' 'With his wooden dagger, in his rage and his anger, he cries ah ha to the devil, like a mad lad: cut your nails, dad; goodbye, Mister Drivel.'

This is the air; that is the glorious sun; / This pearl she gave me, I do feel't and see't: / And though 'tis wonder that enwraps me thus, / Yet 'tis not madness. Where's Antonio, then? / I could not find him at the Elephant; / Yet there he was; and there I found this credit, / That he did range the town to seek me out. / His counsel now might do me golden service; / For though my soul disputes well with my sense, / That this may be some error, but no madness, / Yet doth this accident and flood of fortune / So far exceed all instance, all discourse, / That I am ready to distrust mine eyes / And wrangle with my reason, that persuades me / To any other trust but that I am mad, / Or else the lady's mad; yet if 'twere so, / She could not sway her house, command her followers, / Take and give back affairs and their despatch / With such a smooth, discreet, and stable bearing, / As I perceive she does: there's something in't / That is deceivable. But here comes the lady.

Here is the air, and there the glorious sun; this pearl she gave me I can touch and look at. And though I'm wrapped in wonder like this, it isn't madness. Where's Antonio, then? I couldn't find him at the Elephant, yet he had been there, and I was told that he had gone round the town looking for me. His advice now could be worth gold to me. My soul agrees with my senses that this may be some mistake but not madness; yet this chance event and flood of good fortune so far exceeds any precedent or explanation that I'm ready to distrust my eyes and argue with my reason when it tries to persuade me of anything other than that I'm mad, or else the lady is. Yet if that were so, she couldn't run her house, command her servants, take charge of business and see it carried out with such a smooth, discreet and steady manner as I see she does. There's something deceptive in it. But here comes the lady.

Blame not this haste of mine. If you mean well, / Now go with me and with this holy man / Into the chantry by: there, before him / And underneath that consecrated roof, / Plight me the full assurance of your faith, / That my most jealous and too doubtful soul / May live at peace. He shall conceal it / Whiles you are willing it shall come to note; / What time we will our celebration keep / According to my birth.—What do you say?

Don't blame me for this haste. If your intentions are honourable, come with me now and with this holy man into the chapel nearby. There, in front of him and under that holy roof, give me your full promise of faithfulness, so that my jealous and too anxious soul may live in peace. He will keep it secret until you are willing for it to be made known, and at that time we will hold our celebration in a manner fitting my rank. What do you say?
I'll follow this good man, and go with you; / And, having sworn truth, ever will be true.
I'll follow this good man and go with you, and having sworn to be true, I will always be true.
Then lead the way, good father;—And heavens so shine / That they may fairly note this act of mine!
Then lead the way, good father; and may the heavens shine so that they look kindly on what I am doing!
Now, as thou lovest me, let me see his letter.
Now, if you love me, let me see his letter.
Good Master Fabian, grant me another request.
Good Master Fabian, grant me another request.
Do not desire to see this letter.
Don't ask to see this letter.
This is to give a dog; and in recompense desire my dog again.
That's like giving someone a dog and then asking for the dog back as payment.
Belong you to the Lady Olivia, friends?
Do you belong to Lady Olivia, friends?
Ay, sir; we are some of her trappings.
Yes, sir, we're some of her trimmings.
I know thee well. How dost thou, my good fellow?
I know you well. How are you, my good fellow?
Truly, sir, the better for my foes and the worse for my friends.
Truly, sir, better for my enemies and worse for my friends.
Just the contrary; the better for thy friends.
Just the opposite: better for your friends.

Marry, sir, they praise me and make an ass of me; now my / foes tell me plainly I am an ass: so that by my foes, sir, I / profit in the knowledge of myself, and by my friends I am abused: / so that, conclusions to be as kisses, if your four negatives make / your two affirmatives, why then, the worse for my friends and / the better for my foes.

Well, sir, my friends praise me and make an ass of me, while my enemies tell me plainly that I'm an ass. So through my enemies, sir, I gain in self-knowledge, and through my friends I'm deceived. So, if conclusions are like kisses, where four negatives make two affirmatives, then I'm worse for my friends and better for my enemies.
By my troth, sir, no; though it please you to be one of my / friends.
Honestly, sir, no; though you're pleased to be one of my friends.
Thou shalt not be the worse for me; there's gold.
You won't be worse off because of me. There's some gold.
But that it would be double-dealing, sir, I would you could / make it another.
If it wouldn't be double-dealing, sir, I'd ask you to make it two.
O, you give me ill counsel.
Oh, you're giving me bad advice.
Put your grace in your pocket, sir, for this once, and let / your flesh and blood obey it.
Put your virtue in your pocket, sir, just this once, and let your flesh and blood follow the advice.
Well, I will be so much a sinner to be a double-dealer: there's / another.
Well, I'll be enough of a sinner to be a double-dealer. There's another.

Primo, secundo, tertio, is a good play; and the old saying / is, the third pays for all; the triplex, sir, is a good tripping / measure; or the bells of Saint Bennet, sir, may put you in mind; / one, two, three.

First, second, third is a good game, and the old saying goes, 'Third time pays for all.' Triple time, sir, is a good dancing rhythm; or the bells of Saint Bennet, sir, may remind you: one, two, three.
You can fool no more money out of me at this throw: if you / will let your lady know I am here to speak with her, and bring / her along with you, it may awake my bounty further.
You can't fool any more money out of me with this throw. If you'll let your lady know I'm here to speak with her, and bring her with you, it may wake up my generosity again.

Marry, sir, lullaby to your bounty till I come again. I go, / sir; but I would not have you to think that my desire of having / is the sin of covetousness: but, as you say, sir, let your bounty / take a nap; I will awake it anon.

Well, sir, sing a lullaby to your generosity till I come back. I'm going, sir; but I wouldn't want you to think that my desire to have things is the sin of greed. But, as you say, sir, let your generosity take a nap; I'll wake it up soon.
Here comes the man, sir, that did rescue me.
Here comes the man who rescued me, sir.

That face of his I do remember well: / Yet when I saw it last it was besmeared / As black as Vulcan in the smoke of war: / A bawbling vessel was he captain of, / For shallow draught and bulk unprizable; / With which such scathful grapple did he make / With the most noble bottom of our fleet / That very envy and the tongue of loss / Cried fame and honour on him.—What's the matter?

I remember that face of his well, yet when I last saw it, it was smeared as black as Vulcan's with the smoke of war. He was captain of a trifling ship, worthless for its shallow draught and size, and with it he grappled so destructively with the finest ship of our fleet that even envy and the voices of the losers praised his fame and honour. What's the matter?

Orsino, this is that Antonio / That took the Phoenix and her fraught from Candy: / And this is he that did the Tiger board / When your young nephew Titus lost his leg: / Here in the streets, desperate of shame and state, / In private brabble did we apprehend him.

Orsino, this is the Antonio who seized the Phoenix and all she carried from Crete, and the one who boarded the Tiger in the fight where your young nephew Titus lost a leg. We caught him here in the streets in a private brawl, careless of disgrace or danger.
He did me kindness, sir; drew on my side; / But, in conclusion, put strange speech upon me. / I know not what 'twas, but distraction.
He was kind to me, sir; he drew his sword on my side. But in the end he said strange things to me. I don't know what it was, unless it was madness.
Notable pirate! thou salt-water thief! / What foolish boldness brought thee to their mercies, / Whom thou, in terms so bloody and so dear, / Hast made thine enemies?
Notorious pirate! You salt-water thief! What foolish boldness put you at the mercy of those you made your enemies in such bloody and costly ways?

Orsino, noble sir, / Be pleased that I shake off these names you give me: / Antonio never yet was thief or pirate, / Though, I confess, on base and ground enough, / Orsino's enemy. A witchcraft drew me hither: / That most ingrateful boy there, by your side / From the rude sea's enraged and foamy mouth / Did I redeem; a wreck past hope he was: / His life I gave him, and did thereto add / My love, without retention or restraint, / All his in dedication: for his sake, / Did I expose myself, pure for his love, / Into the danger of this adverse town; / Drew to defend him when he was beset: / Where being apprehended, his false cunning,— / Not meaning to partake with me in danger,— / Taught him to face me out of his acquaintance, / And grew a twenty-years-removed thing / While one would wink; denied me mine own purse, / Which I had recommended to his use / Not half an hour before.

Orsino, noble sir, allow me to reject the names you give me. Antonio has never been a thief or pirate, although, I confess, I had solid grounds to be Orsino's enemy. Witchcraft drew me here. That most ungrateful boy there, by your side, I rescued from the rough sea's angry, foaming mouth. He was a wreck past hope. I gave him his life, and added my love to it, without holding anything back, all devoted to him. For his sake, purely out of love for him, I exposed myself to the danger of this hostile town, and drew to protect him when he was set upon. When I was arrested, his false cunning, since he didn't want to share my danger, taught him to deny he knew me to my face, and in the blink of an eye he became like someone I hadn't seen for twenty years. He refused me my own purse, which I had given him to use not half an hour before.
When came he to this town?
When did he come to this town?
To-day, my lord; and for three months before,— / No interim, not a minute's vacancy,— / Both day and night did we keep company.
Today, my lord; and for three months before that, without a break, not one minute apart, we kept each other company day and night.
Here comes the countess; now heaven walks on earth.— / But for thee, fellow, fellow, thy words are madness: / Three months this youth hath tended upon me; / But more of that anon.—Take him aside.
Here comes the Countess; now heaven walks on earth. But as for you, fellow, fellow, your words are madness. This youth has served me for three months. But more of that later. Take him aside.
What would my lord, but that he may not have, / Wherein Olivia may seem serviceable!— / Cesario, you do not keep promise with me.
What does my lord want, apart from what he can't have, in which Olivia could be of service? Cesario, you're not keeping your promise to me.
What do you say, Cesario?—Good my lord,—
What do you say, Cesario? My good lord...
My lord would speak, my duty hushes me.
My lord wants to speak; my duty keeps me quiet.
If it be aught to the old tune, my lord, / It is as fat and fulsome to mine ear / As howling after music.
If it's anything like the old tune, my lord, it's as gross and sickening to my ear as howling after music.
What! to perverseness? you uncivil lady, / To whose ingrate and unauspicious altars / My soul the faithfull'st offerings hath breathed out / That e'er devotion tender'd! What shall I do?
What, constant in stubbornness? You unkind lady, at whose ungrateful and unpromising altars my soul has breathed out the most faithful offerings that devotion ever made! What shall I do?
Even what it please my lord, that shall become him.
Whatever my lord pleases that suits him.

Why should I not, had I the heart to do it. / Like to the Egyptian thief, at point of death, / Kill what I love; a savage jealousy / That sometime savours nobly.—But hear me this: / Since you to non-regardance cast my faith, / And that I partly know the instrument / That screws me from my true place in your favour, / Live you the marble-breasted tyrant still; / But this your minion, whom I know you love, / And whom, by heaven I swear, I tender dearly, / Him will I tear out of that cruel eye / Where he sits crowned in his master's sprite.— / Come, boy, with me; my thoughts are ripe in mischief: / I'll sacrifice the lamb that I do love, / To spite a raven's heart within a dove.

Why shouldn't I, if I had the heart to do it, like the Egyptian thief at the point of death, kill what I love? A savage jealousy that sometimes has something noble about it. But listen to this. Since you throw my faithfulness aside, and since I partly know the tool that twists me out of my rightful place in your favour, go on living as the marble-hearted tyrant. But this darling of yours, whom I know you love, and whom, I swear by heaven, I hold dear, I'll tear him out of that cruel eye of yours, where he sits crowned in spite of his master. Come with me, boy. My thoughts are ripe for harm. I'll sacrifice the lamb I love, to spite a raven's heart inside a dove.
And I, most jocund, apt, and willingly, / To do you rest, a thousand deaths would die.
And I would die a thousand deaths, most joyfully, readily and willingly, to give you peace.
After him I love / More than I love these eyes, more than my life, / More, by all mores, than e'er I shall love wife; / If I do feign, you witnesses above / Punish my life for tainting of my love!
After the one I love more than I love these eyes, more than my life, more, by every 'more', than I'll ever love a wife. If I'm pretending, you witnesses above, punish my life for staining my love!
Ah me, detested! how am I beguil'd!
Oh, I'm hated! How I've been deceived!
Who does beguile you? who does do you wrong?
Who is deceiving you? Who is wronging you?
Hast thou forgot thyself? Is it so long?— / Call forth the holy father.
Have you forgotten yourself? Has it been so long? Call the holy father.
Whither, my lord? Cesario, husband, stay.
Where to, my lord? Cesario, husband, stay.
Ay, husband, can he that deny?
Yes, husband. Can he deny that?

Alas, it is the baseness of thy fear / That makes thee strangle thy propriety: / Fear not, Cesario, take thy fortunes up; / Be that thou know'st thou art, and then thou art / As great as that thou fear'st—O, welcome, father!

Alas, it's your cowardly fear that makes you strangle your true identity. Don't be afraid, Cesario; accept your good fortune. Be what you know you are, and then you are as great as the man you fear. Oh, welcome, father!

Father, I charge thee, by thy reverence, / Here to unfold,—though lately we intended / To keep in darkness what occasion now / Reveals before 'tis ripe,—what thou dost know / Hath newly passed between this youth and me.

Father, I order you, by your holy office, to reveal here what you know has just taken place between this youth and me, though we meant to keep in the dark what circumstances now reveal before the time is ripe.

A contract of eternal bond of love, / Confirmed by mutual joinder of your hands, / Attested by the holy close of lips, / Strengthen'd by interchangement of your rings; / And all the ceremony of this compact / Sealed in my function, by my testimony: / Since when, my watch hath told me, toward my grave, / I have travelled but two hours.

A contract of eternal love, confirmed by the joining of your hands, witnessed by a holy kiss, strengthened by the exchange of your rings; and all the ceremony of this agreement sealed by me as priest, on my testimony. Since then, my watch tells me, I have travelled only two hours towards my grave.

O thou dissembling cub! What wilt thou be, / When time hath sowed a grizzle on thy case? / Or will not else thy craft so quickly grow / That thine own trip shall be thine overthrow? / Farewell, and take her; but direct thy feet / Where thou and I henceforth may never meet.

Oh, you lying cub! What will you be when time has sprinkled grey on your skin? Or won't your cunning grow so fast that your own tricks trip you up? Goodbye, and take her; but take yourself where you and I may never meet again.
O, do not swear; / Hold little faith, though thou hast too much fear.
Oh, don't swear. Keep a little faith, though you have too much fear.
For the love of God, a surgeon; send one presently to Sir Toby.
For the love of God, a surgeon! Send one to Sir Toby at once.
He has broke my head across, and has given Sir Toby a / bloody coxcomb too: for the love of God, your help: I had rather / than forty pound I were at home.
He's cracked my skull, and bloodied Sir Toby's head as well. For God's sake, help! I'd pay forty pounds to be home right now.
Who has done this, Sir Andrew?
Who has done this, Sir Andrew?
The Count's gentleman, one Cesario: we took him for a / coward, but he's the very devil incardinate.
The Count's gentleman, one Cesario. We thought he was a coward, but he's the devil incarnate.
Od's lifelings, here he is:—You broke my head for / nothing; and that that I did, I was set on to do't by Sir Toby.
God's little life, here he is! You broke my head for nothing; and what I did, Sir Toby put me up to it.
Why do you speak to me? I never hurt you: / You drew your sword upon me without cause; / But I bespake you fair and hurt you not.
Why are you speaking to me? I never hurt you. You drew your sword on me without reason, but I spoke politely to you and didn't hurt you.
If a bloody coxcomb be a hurt, you have hurt me; I think / you set nothing by a bloody coxcomb.
If a bloody head is a hurt, you've hurt me. I suppose you think nothing of a bloody head.
Here comes Sir Toby halting; you shall hear more: but if he had / not been in drink he would have tickled you othergates than he / did.
Here comes Sir Toby limping. You'll hear more. But if he hadn't been drinking, he'd have dealt with you in another way than he did.
How now, gentleman? how is't with you?
That's all one; he has hurt me, and there's the end on't.— / Sot, didst see Dick Surgeon, sot?
It doesn't matter. He's hurt me, and that's the end of it. Fool, have you seen Dick the surgeon, fool?
O, he's drunk, Sir Toby, an hour agone; his eyes were set at / eight i' the morning.
Oh, he's been drunk for an hour, Sir Toby. His eyes were glazed at eight in the morning.
Then he's a rogue. After a passy-measure, or a pavin, I hate a / drunken rogue.
Then he's a rogue and a slow-dancing fool. I hate a drunken rogue.
Away with him. Who hath made this havoc with them?
Take him away! Who has done this damage to them?
I'll help you, Sir Toby, because we'll be dressed together.
I'll help you, Sir Toby, because we'll have our wounds dressed together.
Will you help an ass-head, and a coxcomb, and a knave? a / thin-faced knave, a gull?
Will you help? You ass-head, and fool, and knave? A thin-faced knave, a dupe?
Get him to bed, and let his hurt be looked to.
Get him to bed and have his wound seen to.

I am sorry, madam, I have hurt your kinsman; / But, had it been the brother of my blood, / I must have done no less, with wit and safety. / You throw a strange regard upon me, and by that / I do perceive it hath offended you; / Pardon me, sweet one, even for the vows / We made each other but so late ago.

I'm sorry, madam, that I have hurt your relative. But if he had been my own brother, I couldn't have done less if I wanted to stay safe. You're looking at me strangely, and from that I see it has offended you. Forgive me, sweet one, if only for the promises we exchanged so short a time ago.
One face, one voice, one habit, and two persons; / A natural perspective, that is, and is not.
One face, one voice, one costume, and two people! A natural optical illusion, that is and is not.
Antonio, O my dear Antonio! / How have the hours rack'd and tortur'd me / Since I have lost thee.
Antonio! Oh my dear Antonio! How the hours have racked and tortured me since I lost you!
How have you made division of yourself?— / An apple, cleft in two, is not more twin / Than these two creatures. Which is Sebastian?
How have you divided yourself? An apple split in two is no more alike than these two creatures. Which one is Sebastian?

Do I stand there? I never had a brother: / Nor can there be that deity in my nature / Of here and everywhere. I had a sister / Whom the blind waves and surges have devoured:— / [To Viola.] Of charity, what kin are you to me? / What countryman, what name, what parentage?

Am I standing there? I never had a brother, and I don't have the godlike power to be here and everywhere at once. I had a sister, whom the blind waves and surges have swallowed up. [To Viola] Please tell me, what relation are you to me? What is your country, your name, your family?
Of Messaline: Sebastian was my father; / Such a Sebastian was my brother too: / So went he suited to his watery tomb: / If spirits can assume both form and suit, / You come to fright us.

I'm from Messaline. Sebastian was my father. My brother was a Sebastian too, and he was dressed just like that when he went to his watery grave. If spirits can take on both shape and clothing, you have come to frighten us.

A spirit I am indeed: / But am in that dimension grossly clad, / Which from the womb I did participate. / Were you a woman, as the rest goes even, / I should my tears let fall upon your cheek, / And say—Thrice welcome, drowned Viola!

I am a spirit indeed, but clothed in the solid body I have had since I was born. If you were a woman, since everything else fits, I would let my tears fall on your cheek and say, 'Three times welcome, drowned Viola!'
My father had a mole upon his brow.
My father had a mole on his forehead.
And died that day when Viola from her birth / Had numbered thirteen years.
And he died on the day Viola turned thirteen.
O, that record is lively in my soul! / He finished, indeed, his mortal act / That day that made my sister thirteen years.
Oh, that memory is alive in my soul! He did end his life on the day my sister turned thirteen.

If nothing lets to make us happy both / But this my masculine usurp'd attire, / Do not embrace me till each circumstance / Of place, time, fortune, do cohere, and jump / That I am Viola: which to confirm, / I'll bring you to a captain in this town, / Where lie my maiden weeds; by whose gentle help / I was preserv'd to serve this noble count; / All the occurrence of my fortune since / Hath been between this lady and this lord.

If nothing stands in the way of our happiness except these men's clothes I've taken, don't embrace me until every detail of place, time and fortune fits together and agrees that I am Viola. To confirm it, I'll take you to a captain in this town, where my women's clothes are kept. With his kind help I was saved, to serve this noble Count. Everything that has happened to me since has been between this lady and this lord.

[To Olivia] So comes it, lady, you have been mistook: / But nature to her bias drew in that. / You would have been contracted to a maid; / Nor are you therein, by my life, deceived; / You are betroth'd both to a maid and man.

[To Olivia] So it turns out, lady, that you've been mistaken; but nature followed her natural course in that. You would have been engaged to a girl; but by my life, you aren't deceived in that, because you're engaged to someone who is both a virgin and a man.

Be not amazed; right noble is his blood.— / If this be so, as yet the glass seems true, / I shall have share in this most happy wreck: / [To Viola] Boy, thou hast said to me a thousand times, / Thou never shouldst love woman like to me.

Don't be amazed; his blood is truly noble. If this is so, as the mirror still seems to show, I will share in this most happy shipwreck. [To Viola] Boy, you've said to me a thousand times that you would never love a woman as much as me.
And all those sayings will I over-swear; / And all those swearings keep as true in soul / As doth that orbed continent the fire / That severs day from night.
And I'll swear all those sayings over again, and keep all those oaths as faithfully in my soul as the round sphere of the sky keeps the sun's fire that separates day from night.
Give me thy hand; / And let me see thee in thy woman's weeds.
Give me your hand, and let me see you in your woman's clothes.
The captain that did bring me first on shore / Hath my maid's garments: he, upon some action, / Is now in durance, at Malvolio's suit; / A gentleman and follower of my lady's.
The captain who first brought me ashore has my women's clothes. Because of some legal action he is now in prison, on the complaint of Malvolio, a gentleman who serves my lady.
He shall enlarge him:—Fetch Malvolio hither:— / And yet, alas, now I remember me, / They say, poor gentleman, he's much distract.
He'll release him. Fetch Malvolio here. And yet, alas, now I remember, they say the poor gentleman is out of his mind.
A most extracting frenzy of mine own / From my remembrance clearly banished his.— / How does he, sirrah?
My own distracting madness completely drove his out of my mind. How is he, fellow?

Truly, madam, he holds Belzebub at the stave's end as well / as a man in his case may do: he has here writ a letter to you; I / should have given it you to-day morning, but as a madman's / epistles are no gospels, so it skills not much when they are / delivered.

Truly, madam, he's keeping the devil at arm's length as well as a man in his situation can. He's written a letter to you here. I should have given it to you this morning, but since a madman's letters aren't gospel, it doesn't matter much when they're delivered.
Look then to be well edified when the fool delivers the / madman:—'By the Lord, madam,—'
Then expect to be well instructed when the fool delivers the madman's words. [Reads wildly] 'By the Lord, madam...'
No, madam, I do but read madness: an your ladyship will have / it as it ought to be, you must allow vox.
No, madam, I'm only reading madness. If your ladyship wants it read as it should be, you must allow the proper voice.
Pr'ythee, read i' thy right wits.
So I do, madonna; but to read his right wits is to read / thus; therefore perpend, my princess, and give ear.
I'm doing that, madonna; but to read his sanity is to read like this. So consider, my princess, and listen.

[Reads] 'By the Lord, madam, you wrong me, and the world / shall know it: though you have put me into darkness and given / your drunken cousin rule over me, yet have I the benefit of my / senses as well as your ladyship. I have your own letter that / induced me to the semblance I put on; with the which I doubt not / but to do myself much right or you much shame. Think of me as you / please. I leave my duty a little unthought of, and speak out of / my injury. / The madly-used Malvolio'

[Reads] 'By the Lord, madam, you wrong me, and the world will know it. Though you have shut me in darkness and given your drunken cousin power over me, I still have the use of my senses as well as your ladyship. I have your own letter which persuaded me to put on the appearance I did, and with it I have no doubt I can prove myself right or put you to shame. Think of me as you please. I am forgetting my duty a little, and speak out of my sense of injury. The madly-used Malvolio.'
This savours not much of distraction.
This doesn't sound much like madness.
See him delivered, Fabian: bring him hither.
See that he's released, Fabian. Bring him here.
My lord, so please you, these things further thought on, / To think me as well a sister as a wife, / One day shall crown the alliance on't, so please you, / Here at my house, and at my proper cost.

My lord, if you please, once you have thought these things over, and are happy to think of me as a sister rather than a wife, let one day crown both marriages, if you agree, here at my house and at my own expense.

Madam, I am most apt to embrace your offer.— / [To Viola] Your master quits you; and, for your service done him, / So much against the mettle of your sex, / So far beneath your soft and tender breeding, / And since you called me master for so long, / Here is my hand; you shall from this time be / Your master's mistress.

Madam, I am very ready to accept your offer. [To Viola] Your master releases you; and for the service you've done him, so contrary to your woman's nature, so far beneath your soft and gentle upbringing, and since you called me master for so long, here is my hand. From now on you will be your master's mistress.
Ay, my lord, this same; / How now, Malvolio?
Yes, my lord, this is him. How are you, Malvolio?
Madam, you have done me wrong, / Notorious wrong.
Madam, you have wronged me, shamefully wronged me.

Lady, you have. Pray you peruse that letter: / You must not now deny it is your hand, / Write from it, if you can, in hand or phrase; / Or say 'tis not your seal, not your invention: / You can say none of this. Well, grant it then, / And tell me, in the modesty of honour, / Why you have given me such clear lights of favour; / Bade me come smiling and cross-garter'd to you; / To put on yellow stockings, and to frown / Upon Sir Toby and the lighter people: / And, acting this in an obedient hope, / Why have you suffer'd me to be imprison'd, / Kept in a dark house, visited by the priest, / And made the most notorious geck and gull / That e'er invention played on? tell me why.

Lady, you have. Please read that letter. You can't deny now that it's your handwriting. Write differently from it if you can, in handwriting or style; or say it isn't your seal or your composition. You can't say any of this. Well then, admit it, and tell me, with the decency that honour requires, why you have given me such clear signs of favour, told me to come to you smiling and cross-gartered, to put on yellow stockings, and to frown on Sir Toby and the lesser servants. And when I did this in obedient hope, why have you allowed me to be imprisoned, kept in a dark room, visited by the priest, and made the most notorious idiot and dupe that any trick was ever played on? Tell me why.

Alas, Malvolio, this is not my writing, / Though, I confess, much like the character: / But out of question, 'tis Maria's hand. / And now I do bethink me, it was she / First told me thou wast mad; then cam'st in smiling, / And in such forms which here were presuppos'd / Upon thee in the letter. Pr'ythee, be content: / This practice hath most shrewdly pass'd upon thee: / But, when we know the grounds and authors of it, / Thou shalt be both the plaintiff and the judge / Of thine own cause.

Alas, Malvolio, this isn't my writing, though I admit it's very like my handwriting. But without doubt it's Maria's hand. And now I think about it, it was she who first told me you were mad. Then you came in smiling, and in the very ways the letter had suggested to you. Please, be calm. This trick has been played on you very cruelly; but when we know the reasons and who was behind it, you shall be both the plaintiff and the judge in your own case.

Good madam, hear me speak; / And let no quarrel, nor no brawl to come, / Taint the condition of this present hour, / Which I have wonder'd at. In hope it shall not, / Most freely I confess, myself and Toby / Set this device against Malvolio here, / Upon some stubborn and uncourteous parts / We had conceiv'd against him. Maria writ / The letter, at Sir Toby's great importance; / In recompense whereof he hath married her. / How with a sportful malice it was follow'd / May rather pluck on laughter than revenge, / If that the injuries be justly weigh'd / That have on both sides past.

Good madam, let me speak, and don't let any quarrel or future brawl spoil the happiness of this moment, which I have marvelled at. Hoping it won't, I freely confess that Toby and I set up this trick against Malvolio here, because of some stubborn and discourteous behaviour we resented in him. Maria wrote the letter, because Sir Toby pressed her to, and in reward for it he has married her. The playful malice with which it was carried out should bring laughter rather than revenge, if the injuries on both sides are fairly weighed.
Alas, poor fool! how have they baffled thee!
Alas, poor fool, how they have humiliated you!

Why, 'some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some / have greatness thrown upon them.' I was one, sir, in this / interlude;—one Sir Topas, sir; but that's all one:—'By the / Lord, fool, I am not mad;'—But do you remember? 'Madam, why / laugh you at such a barren rascal? An you smile not, he's / gagged'? And thus the whirligig of time brings in his revenges.

Why, 'some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrown upon them.' I was one of the actors, sir, in this little play: one Sir Topas, sir; but that doesn't matter. 'By the Lord, fool, I am not mad.' But do you remember? 'Madam, why do you laugh at such an empty-headed rascal? Unless you smile, he's dumbstruck.' And so the spinning top of time brings its revenges.
I'll be revenged on the whole pack of you.
I'll be revenged on the whole pack of you.
He hath been most notoriously abus'd.
He has been very shamefully treated.

Pursue him, and entreat him to a peace:— / He hath not told us of the captain yet; / When that is known, and golden time convents, / A solemn combination shall be made / Of our dear souls.—Meantime, sweet sister, / We will not part from hence.—Cesario, come: / For so you shall be while you are a man; / But, when in other habits you are seen, / Orsino's mistress, and his fancy's queen.

Go after him and persuade him to make peace. He hasn't told us about the captain yet. When that is known, and the golden time is right, there will be a solemn union of our dear souls. Meanwhile, sweet sister, we won't leave this place. Cesario, come; for that's what you'll be while you are a man. But when you are seen in other clothes, you will be Orsino's mistress and the queen of his love.

When that I was and a little tiny boy, / With hey, ho, the wind and the rain, / A foolish thing was but a toy, / For the rain it raineth every day. / But when I came to man's estate, / With hey, ho, the wind and the rain, / 'Gainst knave and thief men shut their gate, / For the rain it raineth every day. / But when I came, alas! to wive, / With hey, ho, the wind and the rain, / By swaggering could I never thrive, / For the rain it raineth every day. / But when I came unto my bed, / With hey, ho, the wind and the rain, / With toss-pots still had drunken head, / For the rain it raineth every day. / A great while ago the world begun, / With hey, ho, the wind and the rain, / But that's all one, our play is done, / And we'll strive to please you every day.

When I was a little tiny boy, with hey, ho, the wind and the rain, a foolish thing was just a toy, for it rains, and rains, every day. But when I grew up to be a man, with hey, ho, the wind and the rain, men shut their gates against rogues and thieves, for it rains, and rains, every day. But when I came, alas, to marry, with hey, ho, the wind and the rain, I could never get on by swaggering, for it rains, and rains, every day. But when I came to my bed, with hey, ho, the wind and the rain, I still had a drunken head like the other drinkers, for it rains, and rains, every day. Long, long ago the world was made, with hey, ho, the wind and the rain. No matter: our play is over now, and we'll aim to please you every day.
